articles.title: Stock futures climb as traders try to recover from the S&P 500's losing week: Live updates

paras.en: Stock futures rose early Monday as traders look toward a slew of central bank decisions this week.
S&P 500 futures were up 0.25% while Dow Jones Industrial Average futures added 155 points, or 0.31%. Nasdaq-100 futures gained 0.29%.
The U.S. Federal Reserve, the European Central Bank and the Bank of Japan will announce their rate decisions on Wednesday, Thursday and Friday, respectively.

Asian markets were mixed. Japan's benchmark Nikkei 225 lost 0.1%, but the broad-based Topix was up 0.54%. South Korea's Kospi declined 0.21%, while the the small-cap Kosdaq saw a larger loss, dropping 1.67%. Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index gained 0.66%, and mainland China's CSI 300 was down 0.54%.
Oil prices were lower on Monday in Asia, with Brent futures falling 2.20% to trade at $114.52 a barrel while U.S. West Texas Intermediate slid 2.24% to $101.03 per barrel.
Brent crude had hit its highest level since April last Friday amid news reports that the U.S. and Israel could be planning to launch strikes on Iran after the midterm elections.

Higher oil prices and a broadening sell-off that hit many market sectors dragged the three major averages to losses on Friday. The Dow fell more than 650 points, while the S&P 500 lost 0.5%. The Nasdaq Composite dropped 0.2%
The sell-off also dragged the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq to back-to-back weekly losses.

France, whose 10-year bond yield touched 5% last week for the first time since 2002, got a reprieve from recent turmoil after Moody's decided to maintain its Aa3 credit rating and negative outlook on the nation. Traders feared that the nation, the second-largest economy in the euro zone, would be heading for a downgrade amid its surging borrowing costs.

"A significant and sustained fiscal effort will still be needed beyond the presidential elections of April and May 2027 to bring France's public finances onto stronger footing and stabilise a debt burden that will exceed 120% of GDP in 2027," the agency said Friday.
Moody's added it could upgrade France's outlook to stable if the country's institutions can reduce the deficit.

Traders are awaiting the Federal Reserve's decision on Wednesday. Fed funds futures trading suggests a 90% likelihood that policy makers will hold interest rates at the current target range of 3.75% to 4%.
Bank of America expects the Federal Reserve will raise rates by a quarter percentage point, noting it would be a "heavy lift" move.

"The Oct decision will be a test of Chair Warsh's resolve to bring 'sea change' to the Fed's forward guidance strategy," said Bank of America economist Claudio Irigoyen in a research note. "Warsh's challenge at the presser will be to head off a 'policy error' trade. If the Fed hikes, investors might worry about overtightening. If the Fed holds, markets could question the Fed's inflation-fighting credibility."

articles.title: Oil slides over 2% as traders weigh Saudi attack risks, demand destruction

paras.en: U.S. crude oil fell over 2% on Monday as investors weighed the threat of further attacks on Saudi Arabian energy infrastructure against concerns that elevated prices could eventually erode demand.
U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures slid 2.19% to $101 a barrel, while Brent crude futures declined 1.89% to $114.51 a barrel.
The pullback followed a sharp rally on Friday after attacks by Yemen's Houthi militants on Saudi Arabia reignited fears of disruptions to global energy supplies.

Tensions remained elevated over the weekend as the Houthis said they had targeted Saudi Arabia's main airport in Riyadh and oil facilities on Saturday. Saudi authorities said Sunday that they had intercepted additional missiles and drones.
The kingdom partially resumed operations at its main airport on Sunday despite damage from earlier attacks, even as the Houthis threatened further strikes.

The continued hostilities have heightened concerns about the vulnerability of Saudi Arabia's energy infrastructure, with traders increasingly focused on the risk of a major disruption to production, refining or export facilities.
Speaking to CNBC, Michael Alfaro, chief investment officer at Gallo Partners, estimated that geopolitical uncertainty had already added roughly $20 a barrel to oil prices.
A substantial strike on Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline or additional refining infrastructure could send prices sharply higher, he added, but further gains could eventually undermine consumption.
"What we would likely see if oil pushed above 120, 130, 140 dollars a barrel for Brent, that is, you're going to see more demand destruction," Alfaro said.
Beyond the immediate threat to crude supplies, damage to refining infrastructure could pose a more persistent challenge to global energy markets.
"The real challenge is refining capacity," he said, warning that the disruptions could develop into a longer-term structural problem extending into 2027 and beyond.

Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia plans to begin storing crude oil in Singapore from the second half of 2027, according to energy ministers from both countries, in a move aimed at strengthening the resilience of its Asian supply chain.
In the U.S., the Energy Department on Friday authorized the release of up to 400,000 barrels from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve to address a supply disruption at a Louisiana refinery.
Still, the prospect of additional supply from American producers remains uncertain, with companies reluctant to commit to major new investments amid volatile prices and geopolitical risks.
Alfaro added that U.S. producers were adding some drilling rigs, but remained cautious about substantially increasing capital expenditure.
"We're not really seeing major capex additions to bring new rigs on or bring new production online," he said.

articles.title: ‘Ticking time bomb’: The world's pension funds face an ageing crisis

paras.en: The world's pension systems are confronting a demographic crisis as longer lifespans and dwindling birth rates threaten to stretch retirement finances, raising questions about their ability to sustain payouts for future generations.

Pension offerings generally fall into two categories: defined-benefit plans, which promise retirees a predetermined income, and defined-contribution plans, where payouts depend on accumulated savings and investment returns.

Ageing poses different challenges for the two systems: defined-benefit schemes face mounting liabilities as retirees live longer, while defined-contribution members risk outliving their savings, placing greater pressure on funds' investment performance.

The problem is "huge, and it's gotten more pronounced over time,” said Sebastien Betermier, executive director at the International Centre for Pension Management, noting that some pension funds have members who have been retired for nearly half a century, aged aged 107 or 108.

"The higher the longevity, the more years the pension funds have to cover, and so that immediately comes in as an additional liability," he said. "Think about the cost that it imposes actually on the next generation … it is a ticking time bomb," Betermier told CNBC.

The scale of the challenge is laid bare in the 2026 Marsh CFA Institute Global Pension Index, or MCGPI, report published Tuesday last week. Of the 55 pension systems covered by the index, 43 have fertility rates below the replacement level of 2.1 children per woman, while 23 have rates below 1.5.

Meanwhile, life expectancy at age 65 in more developed regions has increased by 50.9% since 1950 to about 20 additional years, meaning retirement benefits must now last considerably longer. The number of potential workers supporting older people is also set to decline sharply.

“The funding of future pensions and aged care both become more critical as the ratio of workers to retirees continues to decline,” the MCGPI report stated. “Very few systems, as they currently operate, are secure.”

The problem is particularly acute for pay-as-you-go pension systems in which contributions from today's workers largely fund benefits for current retirees, leaving them especially vulnerable to a shrinking workforce.

The pressures are already evident in the U.S., where the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance Trust Fund, which finances retirement and survivor benefits for tens of millions of Americans, is projected to exhaust its reserves in the fourth quarter of 2032, according to its latest trustees' report.
Fully funded pension schemes, which invest contributions from workers and employers to finance future retirement benefits are not immune either.

As their members retire and begin drawing down benefits, some funds could find themselves paying out more than they receive in fresh contributions, forcing them to rethink their investment strategies and liquidity needs, MCGPI cautioned.
“Future benefit outflows will exceed the level of contributions or premiums ... this financial strain will inevitably grow in the future,” the report highlighted.
The demographic crunch is reshaping how pension funds invest, with some taking on greater risks to generate the returns needed to meet growing retirement obligations.
Many mature funds are already paying out more in benefits than they receive in contributions, forcing them to rely increasingly on investment returns and accumulated assets.

In Australia, about a third of superannuation funds recorded negative natural cash flows from assets over a three-year period, meaning benefit payments exceeded contributions, according to a 2025 report by the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority.
Industry watchers say the pressure to generate higher returns has pushed some funds toward riskier and more complex investments, including private equity, infrastructure and private credit.
"You can try to earn higher returns on your investments, but that's going to require taking on greater levels of risk," said Betermier.

Jean-Pierre Aubry, associate director of state and local research at the Center for Retirement Research at Boston College, said pension funds were increasingly shifting toward riskier investments, although the extent varied considerably across markets.
"I think everybody is shifting a little more risk where they can. The costs are going up with this demographic shift," Aubry said.
He pointed to U.S. state and local government pension funds, which hold only about 20% of their assets in bonds, with much of the remainder invested in equities and private assets.
Such allocations make U.S. public pension funds considerably more exposed to investment risk than their counterparts in Europe and Canada, he said.
Not every pension manager sees ageing as a reason to take bigger bets.
David Elias, CEO of Australian pension fund Hostplus said demographic changes were only one of many factors shaping investment decisions.
He stressed the importance of maintaining a diversified portfolio across asset classes, geographies and industries, while ensuring that potential returns adequately compensate for the risks involved.

Elias also said that governments could find ways to mitigate the pressures of ageing populations, including through immigration policies and technological advances, while demographic shifts themselves could create new investment opportunities.
"I don't underestimate governments being incredibly creative in terms of dealing with these types of issues," he said. "You know, but they're going to have to address it, no doubt about that."

articles.title: Strange triangular craft reported in new U.S. government UFO release

paras.en: The Pentagon released yet more documents related to unidentified anomalous phenomena (UAP) on Friday.

This is the seventh tranche of records released since May, though, unlike previous releases, there are no videos or images included. Instead the latest trove is an assortment of memos and reports of encounters with possible UAP.

The most in-depth account is a report from this year in which multiple federal law enforcement agents in an undisclosed location witnessed a UAP “presenting as a matte black triangular shape of extremely low aspect ratio.”

If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.

The object reportedly had a 13- to 15-foot wingspan, measured about six to nine feet in length and had a thickness of one to two feet. According to the agents, the craft was steady as it climbed about 200 or 300 feet into the air above a ridgeline over the course of 10 seconds. At that point, it hovered for another 20 seconds before it flew out of sight at fighter-jet-like speeds into a nearby canyon while hugging the low-lying terrain and executing fluid turns.

The craft didn’t make any of the sounds associated with a fighter jet, however, such as roaring engines or whooshes as it flew through the air. Nor did it display any apparent exhaust plumes or other emissions expected from powered flight. It did show up on an agent’s handheld infrared monocular, however, with a uniform thermal signature across the entire body. According to the report, optical views through binoculars revealed “no propulsive apertures, rotating elements, rivets, panels, windows, canopy, cabin structures, and no protrusions or structural features” on the UAP.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Previous releases have been greeted with skepticism by researchers, who have said that much of what’s been included in those releases was previously seen or had context omitted. But Harvard University professor Avi Loeb, who heads the U.S. government’s UAP Science Advisory Council, said in a blog post that the agents’ newly released story raises questions that could be vital to national defense.

“The fundamental question is whether the triangular object was manufactured in a black project of an adversarial nation or an extraterrestrial project with off-world technology,” he wrote, adding that his current goal for the advisory council is to deploy new sensors in the areas where the UAP were observed.

“As we get higher quality data, we will be able to identify the nature of these mysterious objects,” he wrote. “In collecting better clues, we will either help the Pentagon and the Intelligence Community fulfil their mission of protecting the U.S. from adversaries or discover technology of non-human origin. Investing in the related research is a win-win proposition.”

Friday’s release also included several other witness accounts. Among them was a 1957 Air Force report on an incident involving a B-52 bomber making radar contact with a UAP for five to seven minutes over Saudi Arabia and a 1955 report in which a civilian in California recounted seeing a “very bright and orange” object falling straight down.

articles.title: Warhound wants to engineer and clone military superdogs—can they do it?

paras.en: A new biotechnology start-up wants to use gene-editing technology, cloning and advanced military technology to create a new dog optimized for combat. But does the science to back up its claims exist? And if so, can the company possibly deliver on the idea?

The start-up, called Warhound, is the brainchild of Colossal Biosciences’ Ben Lamm and Anduril Industries’ Palmer Luckey. Warhound intends to clone and genetically modify military service dogs to produce larger, more efficient working dogs for use in conflict zones and policing. Experts say that the science the company proposes is possible—but that it is also prone to error, inefficiencies and a slew of ethical concerns.

Warhound has already biobanked the genetic material from a group of elite service dogs, Lamm says, including breeds such as Belgian Malinois and shepherds. Warhound’s scientists intend to clone the cells of those dogs and edit the cloned embryos to produce new puppies. They’re expecting the first litters in early 2027.

If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.

Cloning dogs is not a new science. Research has shown that cloning service dogs produces puppies that have many of the same desirable traits. But the process can be harmful, says Lisa Moses, a veterinarian and bioethicist at Harvard University. The rate of successful live offspring remains low among the cloned dogs, and the process can put the surrogate mother in danger.

“It is by no means a perfect science, and by that, I mean it’s still a fairly inefficient process,” Moses says. “It requires a lot of dogs to have invasive things done to them and to be killed in order to produce one cloned puppy.”

Warhound intends to make several genetic modifications in its cloned embryos to make the dogs healthier, stronger and better workers. First, the company hopes to modify the dogs to reduce the risk of health conditions such as hip disease, vision loss and cancer predisposition—and, eventually, to optimize ideal traits for military dogs.

“The standard is that no dog enters service carrying a genetic marker known to cause a common career-ending condition,” Lamm says. “From there, we are working on edits specifically targeting additional longevity and health, as well as performance factors.”

Both scientists and private companies have genetically edited dogs before, and the research can “accelerate really fast because genomics in dog breeds already has a lot of data,” says Ben Novak, chief scientist at Revive and Restore, who works on wildlife cloning for conservation. Researchers have edited dogs to tweak genes for hip dysplasia, make them hypoallergenic and treat muscle disease, although the long-term health effects of these changes remain unclear.
But optimizing traits at scale and across service dogs could take time—and leave room for unintended consequences, Novak adds.
“It can be hard to figure out exactly what genetic element is creating a trait,” he says, “and some traits can be the combinations of hundreds or thousands of mutations across genes.”

Colossal Biosciences, which has a stake in Warhound and is providing much of the science, is no stranger to genetic engineering: last year the firm cloned and edited a gray wolf to create an animal that was genetically similar to the extinct dire wolf. The process for Warhound will look similar, Lamm says, but with modern dogs.
In its launch announcement, Warhound said it had raised $200 million in funding. Novak says that from a commercial perspective, the concept makes sense.

“For a biotech company, it is certainly a slam dunk idea: guaranteed military contracts, which is the most funded aspect of U.S. government science, with an actual potential to improve a sector of military use that I think everyone can agree is important.”
But from a bioethics standpoint, Moses says, involving man’s best friend in biotechnology can quickly become fraught.
“I’ve had lots of conversations about what Colossal Biosciences is doing and has done. But when you start messing around with dogs, people feel very differently,” Moses says.

Robert Lanza, former chief scientific officer at the Astellas Institute for Regenerative Medicine and a pioneer of cloning research, says the ethics and technique of Warhound’s premise are far from “black or white.”
“I think such goals are definitely achievable from a scientific perspective. But then again, it’s highly unlikely it could be done without many, many failures and defects,” he says.

articles.title: NASA lays out a packed 14-day schedule for 2027’s Artemis III moon mission

paras.en: NASA’s upcoming Artemis III will be the tiebreaker between two potential lunar landers for future crewed missions to the moon’s surface, the space agency’s head Jared Isaacman said on Friday. But both SpaceX and Blue Origin are planning to touch down on the moon in 2028 no matter what.
Only one will take part in Artemis IV, the 2028 mission to return humans to the lunar surface—NASA will wait as long as possible before making a selection.
Artemis program manager Jeremy Parsons said at a press briefing on Friday that both companies “are planning for lunar landing missions in 2028.”

If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.

Before that, they must get through Artemis III. In that mission, NASA’s Orion crew capsule will attempt to dock with both Blue Origin’s Blue Moon and a version of SpaceX’s Starship. Though no exact launch window was announced, Artemis III is expected to lift off in the summer of 2027, Isaacman said.
Artemis III was previously slated to be a crewed mission to the moon’s surface but was reconfigured earlier this year to instead allow for a complex, two-week-long test run of both landers in orbit.

Artemis III requires several rockets to be in space at once. First, Blue Moon will launch onboard a Blue Origin New Glenn rocket. Once in orbit, tests will be conducted to ensure the lander is in good shape.

Meanwhile NASA’s Orion will already be on the launchpad atop a Space Launch System (SLS) rocket. “We’re going to do everything we can to ensure that that vehicle is ready to go as quickly as we can after that first Blue Origin launch,” Parsons said.
Because the SLS only needs to put Orion into orbit, the rocket has been modified to remove its upper stage.

“When we pivoted to a low-Earth orbit mission, the SLS team quickly came back and said, ‘We don’t need the upper stage for that. Core stage has plenty of performance to drop us in the orbit we need,’” Parsons said.
Three days after Blue Moon launches, Orion will attempt to dock with the spacecraft, after which there will be two days of testing its guidance, navigation and communications systems.

On day six, SpaceX’s Starship will launch, and Orion will detach from Blue Moon, adjust its orbit and attempt a second docking with Starship. The Artemis III crew will not enter Starship during the operation, however, and the test will last just two hours.
“Once Starship operations are complete, Orion and the crew have the remaining days available for additional test objectives before needing to come home,” Parsons said.

Hurdles have to be overcome before any of this can happen: Blue Origin’s New Glenn rocket has not launched since one of the spacecraft exploded spectacularly in May. Parsons said the company expects to resume launches in November and that, right now, NASA has no contingency plans to send Blue Moon to space onboard an alternate vehicle.

“Their design for the Artemis III lander test article is in good shape,” he said. “We have gone through design reviews. We’ve been participating with them, and they have parts coming together from across the United States.”

Meanwhile SpaceX is aiming to conduct another test of Starship next month, which will include upgrades to the craft’s Raptor engines. Starship has seen a number of hiccups, including several explosions during test flights. But in its most recent demonstration, the vehicle was able to enter orbit for the first time—a major milestone on the way to being ready for Artemis III.

Artemis III’s optimal flight timeframe is 14 days, but the mission could be expanded to 17 days if necessary. While the attempted dockings with the landers are key, the mission will also involve collecting vital data on the health of the astronauts.

“Every day of this mission is built around specific tests that reduce risk, give us valuable science and allow us to test out our capabilities before we go and undertake the lunar landing,” Parsons said.
And looking ahead, work has already begun on assembling and testing the Orion crew and service modules that will be used on Artemis IV, Parsons added.

“We are hardly in a position to ‘set it and forget it,’” Isaacman quipped at the event, referring to future Artemis missions planning. “We will never stop listening to data and adapt as circumstances require.”

articles.title: Peek into hidden worlds revealed by the 2026 Nikon Small World contest
articles.author: Allie Skalnik

paras.en: Nestled within a rebuilt inkjet printer, droplets of ink hang suspended above a page. Seen through a microscope, the droplets reveal how an inkjet printer produces crisp, uniform letters.

Ole Bielfeldt, a design student in Cologne, Germany, has been photographing the microscopic world since about 2021. His interest began as a quarantine hobby, when an old school microscope from his attic gave him a way to explore while stuck at home during the pandemic.

His printer image won first place in the 2026 Nikon Small World photomicrography competition. To capture the winning photo, he built a custom rig that moved the paper instead of the printer’s ink nozzles, keeping the nozzles stationary and in focus.

Ole Bielfeldt created this custom rig to catch impossibly fast ink droplets midflight. The contraption is only a bit larger than his head. Swipe through to see what word the printer was spitting out ink to spell.

Bielfeldt estimates that the droplets traveled at nearly 20 meters per second — too fast for even his best slow-motion camera to resolve. To freeze their motion, Bielfeldt worked in darkness, illuminating the scene with a single brief flash. He instructed the printer to repeatedly spell out “macro,” a nod to his social media handle, macrofying.
Before this project, a printer was “like magic,” Bielfeldt says. Photographing its inner workings helped him understand how it operates.
Bielfeldt no longer takes the magic printers spit out for granted. “It’s so, so advanced technically, but at the same time it’s so, so common,” he says.
His photograph is one of 86 images recognized in this year’s competition, whose winners were announced October 21. Here are some of our other favorites.
This pollen-dusted jumping spider offers a close look at the bristling hairs and some of its eight eyes that are easy to miss with the naked eye.

John-Oliver Dum’s fascination with spiders began as a childhood fear. Dum says he suffered a particularly painful arachnid-inflicted bite when he was young. Several years ago, when he was inspired to study the movements of a curly hair tarantula (Tliltocatl albopilosus), Dum became passionate about capturing their beauty.
Preparations for his photographs can begin years before he submits them to a competition. His wife grows plants selected for their pollen, which Dum uses in his images.

“The biggest challenge was finding a spider like this on the right plants, with the right pollen attached to it, at exactly the right time of year and at exactly the right moment,” he says. “You need to understand not only the spider’s behavior, but also the surrounding insect and plant life and their seasonal rhythms.”

Dum hopes the photograph, which won second place, encourages viewers to look more closely, too. “We first have to see the beauty of this largely unknown world before we can truly understand what we may be destroying,” he says.
It’s not a leaf and it’s not a flower. This cross section of a mouse eye is crisscrossed in fractals of blood vessels and tethered by the optic nerve.

Cell biologists Sinem Karaman and Satu Paavonsalo at the University of Helsinki visualize vascular networks, like blood vessels, to study how they work within tissues. The arrangement, Paavonsalo says, could even point to mechanisms underlying how these systems stop working in obesity and diabetes.

Paavonsalo says the duo set out to capture a mouse eye in 3-D, different from the flattened retinas typically used in her research. After meticulous mounting which required several attempts for an arrangement she was satisfied with, Paavonsalo still didn’t know for certain the image would turn out right.

“I had to hope that the sample was correctly positioned and that the staining was detected throughout the sample,” Paavonsalo says, which made her excitement upon seeing the image even more pronounced. The image won 19th place in the competition.
A water bear emerges from its shed cuticle, and oh! What’s that left behind? This egg will be protected by its mother’s discarded skin.

The tardigrade (Hypsibius exemplaris) is one of nature’s toughest creatures, able to survive space by going into a state of suspended animation. This species, emerging from its former skin, is only about two-and-a-half times as wide as a strand of hair. Evolutionary developmental biologist Gonzalo Quiroga-Artigas captured the image during his studies of these tiny wonders at the University of Montpellier in France.

In the tardigrade life cycle, “egg laying is closely synchronized with molting,” says Quiroga-Artigas. Tardigrades can lay up to about a dozen eggs at once, and the moment one sheds its old cuticle happens quickly enough that it’s easy to miss.

Snapping this image demanded painstaking mounting and imaging of many specimens. Quiroga-Artigas chose this particular one, which won 12th, because “the egg looks almost like a precious gem being left behind by its mother.”

This slime mold (Hemitrichia sp.) was found in the heart of Brooklyn, N.Y., sprouting from a decaying log in Prospect Park. The image features the mold’s gelatinous fruiting bodies, which release spores as part of reproduction. To bring the delicate structures into sharp detail, Eric Epstein stacked 240 images.

First, Epstein searched local parks for slime molds to photograph, carefully cutting pieces of waterlogged wood free without disturbing his subjects. “In this liquidy state, any touch would demolish” the fruiting bodies, he says.

One species of slime mold closely mirrors the cosmic web of gas and dark matter connecting galaxies, which helps scientists to more accurately map the cosmos. Another species has fascinated researchers for its ability to pack a store of bacteria to feed the next generation, when it’s near death.
Epstein hopes the photograph hints “at [a] vast array of activity beyond our unaided perception.” The image won sixth place in the competition.
This cell could have become anything in the body. Through some scientific nudging, it burst into a brilliant neuron.

Clusters of nuclei, looking like flashpoints in an intricate web, were captured by undergraduate student Faith Fernandes and structural cell biologist James Glover at the University of California, Berkeley.

The image commemorates the team’s first attempt at crafting neurons from a particular kind of stem cell. “I was so instantly enamored with this piece that I made it my computer wallpaper as soon as it was taken,” Fernandes says.

The eruption of color depicts human induced pluripotent stem cells, which can become any type of cell in the body, that have developed into neurons. The neurotubules, which contribute to the structure of and transportation of intracellular molecules, appear blue. Orange indicates where the DNA is located.

The stem cells are created by reprogramming adult cells to a stage before the cell was locked into a path to become a specific type of cell. They are studied for their many potential applications in regenerative medicine.

Fernandes says she hopes that studying these cells will illuminate ways to address neurodegeneration in diseases such as Parkinson’s disease. Already, researchers have used these cells to regrow eye tissue, address premature aging in mouse studies and grow organs. The shot won an Image of Distinction title in the competition.

articles.title: A lifesaving medication is not behind the drop in U.S. overdose deaths
articles.author: Aimee Cunningham

paras.en: Drug overdose deaths unexpectedly took a nosedive in the United States a few years ago. But it doesn’t appear to be due to more people being revived than before.

At the peak in mid-2023, there were around 111,000 drug overdose deaths per year in the United States. By the end of 2025, the number had fallen to under 71,000 per year, and researchers are still piecing together why. One theory: The wider availability of naloxone, a medication that reverses opioid overdoses, made it possible to revive more people than before.

But a study of U.S. emergency medical services agencies found that emergency medical responses for nonfatal overdoses dropped along with deaths, and the use of naloxone also declined. That suggests that fewer overdoses overall occurred, not that naloxone stopped deaths more often, researchers report October 21 in the Journal of the American Medical Association.

“Naloxone still saves lives every day,” says Michael Barnett, a health services researcher at Brown University School of Public Health in Providence, R.I. “But it doesn’t look like the reason for the sudden turn” in overdose deaths.
State policies, community distribution programs and the U.S. Food and Drug Administration’s approval of the nasal spray version of naloxone as an over-the counter drug have expanded access.

Barnett and colleagues analyzed nearly 186 million emergency medical service activations — an ambulance or other EMS response after a 911 call — nationwide that occurred from May 2020 through December 2025. Of 2.5 million responses for nonfatal drug overdoses, 40.5 percent involved opioids.

From May of 2023 onward, EMS activations for nonfatal opioid overdoses fell on average by about 6,000, or around 33 percent, below what was expected. Total administrations of naloxone dropped as well, by around 4,700 on average, or 21 percent below what was expected. The study suggests that naloxone was not used more often than before by bystanders prior to the EMS response, but did not include data on cases when a bystander provided naloxone and no one called 911.

Additional possibilities to explain the steep drop in overdose deaths — which followed a three-decade increase — include changes to the illicit opioid supply or with the population of people at risk for overdoses. “My own read is that a disruption in the fentanyl supply best explains how sudden and widespread the turn was,” Barnett says. “Underneath it, the population at risk has probably been shrinking for years.”

But “a supply-driven decline can reverse,” Barnett says, noting that the decline in overdose deaths slowed in 2025. Traffickers can adapt “by finding new chemical sources or turning to more potent synthetic opioids.”

articles.title: Why did humans’ brains surpass chimps’? A tiny foe might help explain it
articles.author: Jake Buehler

paras.en: Viruses may be minuscule, but one could have influenced major differences between human and chimpanzee brains.

Millions of years ago, a virus left DNA behind in an African ape’s genome, and the genetic material stuck around in modern day chimps. Those ghosts of infections past appear to influence genes involved in neuron development, which may help explain how human and chimp brains ended up so different, researchers report October 23 in Science Advances.

Compared with the brains of their chimpanzee kin, human brains are three times larger and more cognitively powerful. Yet “most of their protein-making genes are very similar,” says Johan Jakobsson, a neuroscientist at Lund University in Sweden. In the absence of large differences in the genetic code, Jakobsson and his colleagues decided to look at the parts of the human and chimp genome that control when and where genes are turned on or off.

Changes in gene regulation can come from viruses. Some viruses called retroviruses insert their own DNA into their hosts’ genomes to command host cells to build more viruses. But those parasitic bits of DNA can linger long after an infection. If this happens in reproductive cells, the viral DNA gets passed down with the host’s DNA.

These leftover bits, called endogenous retroviruses, no longer code for the production of infectious viruses, but they can have a big impact on the host’s biology — especially if they make copies of themselves across the genome. And they have. Such viral remnants make up at least 8 percent of the genomes of humans and chimps alike. More generally, these DNA leftovers have been linked with some major evolutionary events, such as the evolution of the mammalian placenta.

Jakobsson and his colleagues focused on a particular viral vestige in chimps. The holdover came from an infection in an ancestral African ape somewhere between 5 million and 7 million years ago. In chimpanzees, the viral DNA had stuck itself into the genome at 158 different locations. However, it is curiously absent in humans. It’s still unknown why.

The researchers wanted to know how that exact pathogen footprint might affect chimpanzees’ brains compared with those of humans. Working with chimpanzee stem cells, they removed the viral DNA using CRISPR, a gene editing technology that allows for precise, targeted cuts in DNA. Once the viral DNA was gone, a nearby gene called LINC00662 — normally silenced in chimpanzees — turned on, making RNA the team could detect. This matches the normal condition in human brain cells, in which LINC00662 is active. The team also used CRISPR to shut off LINC00662 in the human cells, matching the silenced condition seen in chimpanzees.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: When LINC00662 was active in chimp or human cells, the researchers noticed activity boosts to other genes that may be important to brain development — such as genes involved in the development and maturation of neurons and in making new neural connections. It’s not yet clear exactly how the viral DNA’s shutdown of this brain gene network affected the biology of chimpanzee brains. However, this genetic difference may have contributed to a divergence in how human and chimpanzee brains evolved, Jakobsson says. “Our findings show one way an ancient viral [DNA] insertion could create a lasting difference in how a gene is regulated in humans and chimpanzees,” Jakobsson says. Other genetic and environmental changes could be involved in the puzzle as well, he says.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Researchers have previously looked to single letter swaps in DNA to help explain how humans and chimp brains drifted apart in their evolution. But the new study highlights that creatures can rack up genome changes in other ways, says Giorgia Modenini, an evolutionary biologist at the University of Padua in Italy who was not involved with this research.

The researchers do a convincing job of showing that these particular viral leftovers influence developmental differences between human and chimp neurons, says Ravinder Kanda, an evolutionary geneticist at Oxford Brookes University in Oxford, England. “They’ve proved that absolutely. How far that goes, I don’t think we can quite say yet.”

It could be that other controls on genes’ activity are also involved or that this particular ancient lever-puller may represent just a sliver of the viral holdovers that have shaped brain development, Kanda says. “I think there are many, many more retroviruses to be discovered, and at the moment we’ve only touched the tip of the iceberg.”

articles.title: Scientists Discovered an Amazing Practical Use For The World's Leftover Coffee Grounds
articles.author: Tessa Koumoundouros

paras.en: Charred coffee grounds could make concrete up to 30 percent stronger, scientists in Australia have found.
Their clever recipe could solve multiple problems at once.
Each year, the world produces about 10 billion kilograms (22 billion pounds) of coffee waste, most of which ends up in landfills.

"The disposal of organic waste poses an environmental challenge as it emits large amounts of greenhouse gases, including methane and carbon dioxide, which contribute to climate change," explained RMIT University engineer Rajeev Roychand when the research was first published in 2023.
With a booming construction market globally, there's an ever-increasing demand for resource-intensive concrete, causing another set of environmental challenges.
Watch the video below for a summary of the study:

"The ongoing extraction of natural sand around the world – typically taken from river beds and banks – to meet the rapidly growing demands of the construction industry has a big impact on the environment," said RMIT engineer Jie Li.

"There are critical and long-lasting challenges in maintaining a sustainable supply of sand due to the finite nature of resources and the environmental impacts of sand mining. With a circular-economy approach, we could keep organic waste out of landfill and also better preserve our natural resources like sand."
Organic products like coffee grounds can't be added directly to concrete because they leak chemicals that weaken the building material's strength.
So using low energy levels, the team heated coffee waste to over 350 °C (around 660 °F) while depriving it of oxygen.

This process is called pyrolysis. It breaks down the organic molecules, resulting in a porous, carbon-rich charcoal called biochar that can form bonds with and thereby incorporate itself into the cement matrix.
Roychand and colleagues also tried pyrolyzing the coffee grounds at 500 °C, but the resulting biochar particles were not as strong.
The researchers cautioned that they still need to assess the long-term durability of their cement product.
They're now working on testing how the hybrid coffee-cement performs under freeze/thaw cycles, water absorption, abrasions, and many more stressors.
The team is also working on creating biochars from other organic waste sources, including wood, food, and agricultural.

"Our research is in the early stages, but these exciting findings offer an innovative way to greatly reduce the amount of organic waste that goes to landfill," said RMIT engineer Shannon Kilmartin-Lynch.

"Inspiration for my research, from an Indigenous perspective, involves Caring for Country, ensuring there's a sustainable life cycle for all materials and avoiding things going into landfill to minimize the impact on the environment."
Related: One Way of Drinking Coffee Could Help You Live Longer, Study Finds

In 2024, RMIT and Macedon Ranges Shire Council poured a world-first real-world trial: a footpath in Gisborne, Victoria, made with the coffee biochar concrete alongside a wood-chip-biochar section and a standard-concrete control section.

Later that year, Victoria's Big Build used coffee-biochar concrete for a footpath on the Pakenham Roads Upgrade – the first major infrastructure project to use it – with contractor BildGroup estimating the job diverted roughly 140,000 coffees' worth of grounds from landfill and saved more than 3 metric tons (3.3 US tons) of sand.

In early 2025, the RMIT team picked up the People's Choice Problem Solver Award at Universities Australia's Shaping Australia Awards, and said they were working with a commercialization partner to build a business case to bring the material to market.
Their research was published in the Journal of Cleaner Production.

articles.title: Women Appear to Experience Psychedelic Drugs More Intensely, And We Don't Know Why
articles.author: Esra Öz

paras.en: Magic mushrooms can make colors appear more vivid, alter the sense of time, and send thoughts in unfamiliar directions.
The compound responsible for these effects is called psilocybin, but there's still a lot we don't understand about how it works.
Psilocybin is of interest to scientists because of its potential to help treat mental health conditions under controlled conditions.
One question that remains to be solved is whether women and men have different experiences when they take the drug.
Knowing what someone might experience is important for preparing them beforehand and supporting them during a session.

In a new preprint study that has not yet undergone peer review, researchers from Maastricht University in the Netherlands found that women reported feeling some effects more strongly than men, though not all of them.
"What surprised me most was that these differences were selective," Natasha Mason, who studies how drugs affect the brain and behavior, told ScienceAlert.
Mason and fellow Maastricht researcher Eline Haijen-Bongers led a team that combined results from two trials involving 40 women and 32 men.
All were healthy volunteers with previous experience of drugs that alter perception and thought, known as psychedelics.
The volunteers did not eat mushrooms. They took psilocybin made in a laboratory.
The first trial compared it with another manufactured drug that changes perception and mood, called 2C-B. Participants received both drugs and an inactive substance on separate days.
The second trial examined LSD, another laboratory-made psychedelic. It was also compared with an inactive substance, or placebo.
Neither the volunteers nor the researchers working directly with them knew which substance they were receiving.
Participants rated how they felt throughout the sessions and answered questions about their experiences afterward. Researchers also collected blood samples.

Because some of the volunteers participated in both the trials, the 72 participants contributed 94 active-drug sessions altogether. The team's analysis took into account that the data in both trials came from the same people.
When the results were compared, women reported feeling more strongly under the influence. They also described greater reductions in alertness and felt less able to control their thinking.

Several differences remained after the researchers accounted for age differences between women and men. The difference in feeling under the influence was most pronounced with psilocybin. Reduced alertness differed significantly with psilocybin and 2C-B, but not with LSD.
Tests of understanding and responding emotionally to other people found no significant sex differences.

One possible explanation was body weight. Each drug was given at a fixed dose regardless of participants' weight. Because women in the study generally weighed less, the same dose could potentially produce higher drug concentrations in their blood.
But the blood measurements did not show this. Neither peak drug concentrations nor overall exposure during the measured period differed significantly between women and men.

The researchers are therefore considering other possibilities, including hormones. These drugs affect a brain signaling system involving a chemical messenger called serotonin. Hormones such as estrogen can also influence how that system works.
A separate review by members of the same Maastricht team, published in Molecular Psychiatry, explores these possible connections.
"That said, we did not measure hormone levels or account for menstrual cycle phase in this study, so we cannot determine whether hormones contributed to the differences we observed," Mason explained.

As scientists investigate how psychedelics affect the brain, understanding that people may need different support could help shape future treatments. The findings first need to be tested in larger studies and in patients receiving treatment.

Neither trial was originally designed to investigate sex differences. The sample was small, and the analysis did not adjust for the greater chance of false-positive findings when making multiple comparisons.
"It would certainly be premature to conclude that women need lower doses of psychedelics, or that they respond better or worse to psychedelic therapy," Mason cautioned.
The study did not investigate long-term therapeutic benefits.
The findings are reported in a preprint paper available at bioRxiv.

articles.title: World-First Cancer Vaccine Cuts Melanoma Recurrence or Death Risk by 42% in Landmark Trial
articles.author: Carly Cassella

paras.en: It's been 20 years since Australian researchers created the world's first vaccine developed specifically to prevent cancer.
Thanks to the HPV vaccine, Australia is on track to become one of the first nations in the world to eliminate cervical cancer.
Now, research led by scientists Down Under has made another breakthrough – this time for skin cancer.

The first personalized mRNA cancer vaccine has now succeeded in a phase 3 clinical trial, reducing the risk of melanoma returning or causing death by 42 percent compared with standard immunotherapy alone.
The results are even better than scientists were expecting.
The global principal investigator, medical oncologist Georgina Long from Melanoma Institute Australia (MIA), presented the results at the European Society for Medical Oncology Congress 2026.
They are set to be published in the New England Journal of Medicine.
"These findings are a foundational shift in our approach to cancer: harnessing the immune system in a more personalized way to reduce the risk of melanoma recurrence or death," says Long.
"This has not been achieved before in the history of cancer drug development."

Medical oncologist Robert Vonderheide, president-elect of the American Association for Cancer Research, who was not involved in the trial, told The New York Times the trial's results are up there with "our biggest breakthroughs."
The mRNA vaccine was developed by Moderna and Merck, and it is designed to stop melanoma from coming back after surgery.
First, researchers sequence the tumor from each patient, and then they figure out what separates the 'fingerprint' of this tumor from other, healthy cells in the body.
A vaccine based on that information essentially creates a personalized 'wanted poster' of the cancer for the patient's own immune system.
"This is delivered as mRNA, so the body's own cells display the poster to the immune system, showing it exactly what to look out for and attack," says Long.
The medicine works in conjunction with an existing immunotherapy called Keytruda (pembrolizumab).
"Cancer can fool the immune system with a fake friendly handshake, so the immune system thinks the cancer cell is normal," explains Long.
"Pembrolizumab blocks the handshake, allowing immune cells to recognize the cancer and attack it, but it is the same drug for everyone."
Personalizing a treatment to use alongside pembrolizumab seems to improve the results.
The phase 3 clinical trial involved more than 1,100 patients from 157 sites around the world, and the results back up impressive findings from a phase 2 trial, published in 2024.
For patients who remained cancer-free six months after starting treatment, the risk reduction for melanoma recurrence or death was 58 percent compared with pembrolizumab alone.
The mRNA vaccine is not yet available to patients in Australia or the United States, but the results have entered a regulatory review process.
That could take several years, depending on the nation.
In Australia, which has one of the highest melanoma rates in the world, one person dies from this cancer every 6 hours.
A vaccine that could stop the cancer from recurring could save numerous lives.
And it's not just skin cancer that could benefit from mRNA technology.
"Having succeeded in melanoma, this proof of concept could mark the beginning of a foundational shift in how we treat cancer, helping patients remain cancer-free for longer," says Long.
Alex Menzies, a medical oncologist at MIA, agrees.

"The hope for the near future is that it may not only improve outcomes for melanoma patients with advanced disease, but also those with other types of cancer where current immunotherapies are poorly effective," Menzies explains.
That's an exciting idea, but there is still more work to be done.
Recently, several randomized trials testing mRNA vaccines for colorectal cancer and for head and neck cancer have failed to reduce recurrence.
That makes these newest results even more important.

"The INTerpath-001 trial shows that treatment built from the unique signature of a patient's own tumor, working alongside checkpoint inhibitor immunotherapy, can sharpen the immune system to find and destroy any remaining cancer cells," says Long.
"Just as email transformed how we communicate, individualized neoantigen therapy has the potential to transform how we treat cancer."

articles.title: New evidence suggests spinosaurus spent most of its life underwater

paras.en: New evidence suggests spinosaurus spent most of its life underwater

- Millions of years after animals first conquered land, some took an extraordinary evolutionary U-turn and returned to the water. Using machine learning and thousands of fossil measurements, Yale scientists have uncovered surprising clues about which prehistoric creatures truly became aquatic. Their findings suggest that Spinosaurus spent most of its life underwater, while some ancient marine reptiles previously thought to be fully aquatic actually spent considerable time on land.

For millions of years, evolution helped animals make the transition from life in the ocean to life on land. But the journey did not always move in one direction. Many species eventually returned to the water, developing new adaptations that allowed them to thrive in aquatic environments.

Dozens of major groups of mammals and reptiles made this remarkable evolutionary reversal. Now, a new study from Yale University is shedding light on when and how these transitions occurred, as well as which ancient animals became fully aquatic and which continued to depend on land.
The findings were published in the journal Current Biology.

"These secondarily aquatic groups adapted in strikingly similar ways to their new aquatic home -- evolving flippers and a suite of other features that made them better swimmers," said lead author Caleb Gordon, who completed his doctorate at Yale's Graduate School of Arts and Sciences (GSAS) earlier this year and is now a postdoctoral researcher at the Florida Museum of Natural History. "As a result, they've become textbook examples of convergent evolution, which can tell us a lot about the processes driving and constraining adaptive change in response to similar environmental cues."
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Using Ancient Fossils and AI to Reconstruct Evolution

To investigate these evolutionary changes, the researchers examined hundreds of fossil and modern specimens housed at the Yale Peabody Museum and dozens of other institutions worldwide. They collected extensive new data, including measurements (more than 11,000), photographs, and CT scans.

The team combined traditional paleontological techniques with machine learning models that account for evolutionary relationships. They also incorporated a statistical approach originally used by naval forces during World War II. Together, these methods offered a new way to investigate one of the most remarkable transitions in vertebrate evolution.

"Reconstructing the lives of extinct life forms in a scientifically rigorous way, as opposed to just telling stories, is a precise and delicate undertaking," said Bhart-Anjan Bhullar, senior author of the study. Bhullar is an associate professor of Earth and planetary sciences in Yale's Faculty of Arts and Sciences (FAS) and an associate curator of vertebrate paleontology and vertebrate zoology at the Peabody Museum.

"It requires a careful interweaving of data from modern organisms, of which our understanding is necessarily far deeper, and knowledge of these living organisms' genealogy relative to fossil forms," he said. "Caleb's work accomplishes all of this and more, and on a massive evolutionary scale."

For decades, scientists have disagreed about when particular groups of prehistoric animals became fully adapted to life underwater. The fossil record often provides incomplete or conflicting clues, making it difficult to determine whether an extinct species primarily lived on land, in water, or in both environments.

Some skeletal features may indicate an aquatic lifestyle, while others suggest that the same animal remained capable of moving and feeding on land. These contradictions have led researchers to different conclusions about how ancient species behaved.
"In these cases, paleontologists are often stuck, as different lines of evidence disagree about what the ancient animal was like," Gordon said.

To address this uncertainty, Gordon developed a method using relatively simple but effective machine learning models trained on living animals. By identifying relationships between skeletal proportions and known lifestyles, the models can estimate how extinct species used aquatic environments. They can also predict soft tissue adaptations, including swimming structures that rarely survive in fossils.
Spinosaurus May Have Spent Most of Its Life Underwater
One of the most striking findings concerns Spinosaurus, a giant prehistoric dinosaur whose relationship with water has generated considerable controversy.

Spinosaurus lived approximately 113 million to 94 million years ago in what is now northern Africa. Although scientists generally agree that it was associated with aquatic environments, exactly how it moved, hunted, and spent its time remains a subject of debate.

Some evidence points to an animal that frequently submerged itself and pursued prey underwater, much like seals or penguins. Other findings suggest a lifestyle closer to that of a modern heron, with Spinosaurus walking and searching for food along shorelines and in shallow water.
The Yale team's analysis provides new support for the more aquatic interpretation.

"Our results shed new light on how much time Spinosaurus spent submerged, which could support the underwater hunting view," Gordon said. "We confidently recovered highly aquatic habits for Spinosaurus, indicating that it spent the vast majority of its time submerged in the water."
Although the findings do not settle every question about how Spinosaurus hunted, they strengthen the case that this enormous predator spent much more of its life underwater than on land.
Ancient Marine Reptiles That Never Fully Left Land

The researchers reached a different conclusion about mesosaurs, small marine reptiles that lived between 290 million and 274 million years ago in regions now forming parts of South Africa and eastern South America.

Mesosaurs have long interested paleontologists because they gave birth to live young, a characteristic some researchers have interpreted as evidence of a fully aquatic existence. However, the new analysis suggests that their limbs were not adapted for a life spent entirely in water.
Instead, their skeletal proportions indicate that mesosaurs regularly moved between aquatic and terrestrial environments.
"They spent a lot of time on land, like a modern-day alligator or platypus does," Gordon said. "Mesosaurs didn't completely leave the land behind."

The findings also suggest a broader pattern among the earliest marine reptiles. According to the researchers, all Paleozoic marine reptiles (all marine reptiles around before the dinosaurs appeared) continued to return to land regularly. None appeared to have evolved a completely aquatic lifestyle, with even the most water adapted species remaining amphibious.

The researchers found that forelimb proportions were particularly useful for distinguishing these lifestyles. Using this information, their models could predict with more than 90% accuracy whether an animal possessed soft tissue flippers and whether it had highly or fully aquatic habits.
A World War II Technique Helps Solve an Evolutionary Mystery
An especially unusual part of the research involved adapting a statistical method developed during the 1940s.

"Caleb resurrected a statistical technique from a bygone era," said co-author Jacques Gauthier, a professor of Earth and planetary sciences at Yale and curator-in-charge for vertebrate paleontology at the Peabody Museum. "It was developed during WWII to estimate the probability that an approaching blip on the radar screen was an enemy plane. Caleb cleverly used it to get at whether or not an extinct animal had limbs modified for swimming."
By repurposing this approach, the researchers could assess the likelihood that an extinct species possessed specialized swimming adaptations, even when direct evidence of those features was missing.

The method could eventually help scientists investigate other major changes in evolutionary history. Potential applications include studying when human ancestors developed the ability to walk on two legs and how the dinosaur ancestors of birds evolved the ability to fly.

Because most prehistoric vertebrates are known primarily through their fossilized skeletons, reconstructing their behavior is one of paleontology's greatest challenges. Bones preserve valuable information, but they rarely provide a complete picture of how an animal lived.

Traditionally, scientists have interpreted particular skeletal features to make arguments about the lifestyles of extinct species. Those interpretations can differ significantly, especially when fossils are incomplete or several anatomical characteristics point toward different conclusions.
The new approach offers a more systematic way to evaluate that evidence, using patterns observed in living species to make testable predictions about animals that disappeared millions of years ago.

"Bones are all that is left to us of the vast majority of vertebrate animals that have lived on Earth," Bhullar said. "We want to know so very much about these creatures and the succession of lost worlds they inhabited, but we have so little on which to base our conclusions. From skeletal remains, people have tried to discern life habits, generally making an argument on the basis of one preferred set of features or another. Caleb's method removes the subjectivity from this process and allows the data to speak for themselves."

articles.title: Scientists overcome a hidden obstacle to more powerful quantum computers

paras.en: Scientists overcome a hidden obstacle to more powerful quantum computers

- Scientists have discovered a way to operate multiple silicon qubits simultaneously with remarkable accuracy, overcoming a major challenge in scaling up quantum computers. Their new technique maintained accuracy of approximately 99.9% even when all five qubits were running at once, opening the door to larger and more powerful quantum processors.

Silicon spin qubits could play a major role in the future of quantum computing because they can be produced using the same semiconductor manufacturing methods that make today's computer chips. However, researchers have faced a significant challenge. When multiple silicon qubits are controlled at the same time, their operations tend to become less accurate. Building practical, large quantum computers will require scientists to control many qubits simultaneously while keeping errors to a minimum.

Researchers at the RIKEN Center for Emergent Matter Science and their collaborators have now made important progress toward solving this problem. In a study published in Nature Physics, the team demonstrated highly accurate control of several silicon spin qubits operating simultaneously. Their experiments used an array of five qubits connected to a shared microwave control line. By identifying a major cause of errors during simultaneous operation, the scientists developed a technique to reduce those errors and maintain precision.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Leon Camenzind, a RIKEN research scientist and co-first author who supervised the experiments, explains the significance of the results: "This shows that high-fidelity control can be maintained even when several qubits are operated at the same time and represents an important step toward scaling up silicon-based quantum processors."
Scientists Identify a Hidden Source of Quantum Computing Errors

Unlike conventional computers, which store information as bits representing either 0 or 1, quantum computers use quantum bits, or qubits, that can exist in combinations of both states. Silicon spin qubits store this information using the spin of individual electrons confined within silicon. Performing reliable quantum calculations requires extremely precise control over these electron spins.

Microwave signals provide that control, but operating multiple qubits simultaneously can create unwanted effects that interfere with their accuracy. The researchers traced much of this problem to a phenomenon called the AC Stark shift.

This effect occurs when microwave control signals alter a qubit's effective energy levels, producing changes in the phase of its quantum state. Those phase shifts can disrupt the intended operation of individual qubits, particularly when several are being controlled at once.

To counteract the problem, the team created a calibration method that compensates for these unwanted shifts. Rather than separately calibrating every possible combination of qubits, the technique relies on calibrations performed between pairs of qubits. This makes the approach more practical for systems containing larger numbers of quantum bits.

"Rather than requiring an entirely separate calibration procedure for every possible combination of qubits, our method uses calibrations between pairs of qubits to compensate for the unwanted phase shifts," explains Yi-Hsien Wu, the first author who carried out the experiments as part of his PhD research.
Quantum Qubits Achieve Accuracy Above 99.99%

The researchers combined their calibration technique with an improved device design and carefully adjusted microwave control pulses. Their results showed that exceptionally high accuracy could be maintained even when multiple qubits were operating simultaneously.

When the five qubits were tested individually, each achieved single-qubit gate fidelity well above 99.99%, with the highest approaching 99.999%. Fidelity describes how closely a quantum operation matches its intended result.

The team then tested how well the system performed when several qubits were active together. With as many as three qubits operating simultaneously, fidelity remained above 99.99%. Even when all five qubits were controlled at once, accuracy stayed at approximately 99.9%, approaching the levels needed for practical fault-tolerant quantum computing.

Although the calibration method greatly reduced errors, it did not eliminate them entirely. The researchers found that the remaining loss of accuracy was linked to drive-induced decoherence, an effect caused by the greater microwave power required to operate multiple qubits simultaneously.
Unlike the unwanted phase shifts corrected by the new technique, decoherence involves the loss of the delicate quantum coherence needed for reliable operations.
According to Camenzind, "This is a limitation, but further improvements to device design could help mitigate this source of error."
A New Path Toward Larger Quantum Processors

The findings show that controlling several silicon spin qubits at the same time does not necessarily require a major sacrifice in accuracy. By correcting a key source of errors, the researchers have demonstrated a promising approach for operating more qubits through shared microwave control lines.

This is especially important for the development of large quantum processors. Giving every qubit its own independent control system would make increasingly complex devices difficult to manage. Shared control lines could offer a more practical way to expand these systems while maintaining the precision needed for quantum calculations.

"By addressing a key source of control errors through pairwise calibration," says Camenzind. "Our study supports the use of shared control lines as a practical approach to scaling up quantum processors. Combined with silicon's compatibility with established semiconductor manufacturing, we believe that this advance could help pave the way toward larger quantum processors capable of performing increasingly complex computations."

The broader objective is to develop quantum computers that can reliably perform calculations despite the errors and disturbances that affect quantum systems. Such machines, known as fault-tolerant quantum computers, will require precise, dependable control over large numbers of qubits.

"Our long-term goal is to build a fault-tolerant quantum computer based on silicon spin qubits, and reliable parallel control is an essential step toward that goal," adds Seigo Tarucha, project manager of a silicon quantum computing project under JST's Moonshot Goal 6.
