articles.title: A simple liquid can stop cavities without drilling, major study confirms

paras.en: A simple liquid can stop cavities without drilling, major study confirms

- A simple liquid painted onto teeth in seconds can stop cavities without drilling, injections, or anesthesia, according to a major clinical trial involving young children. The inexpensive treatment could spare thousands of children painful dental procedures and surgery while paving the way for broader FDA-approved use.

A cavity doesn't always have to mean drilling, injections, or an uncomfortable visit to the dentist. A major clinical trial has confirmed that a simple, inexpensive liquid can stop tooth decay in young children, potentially preventing painful infections and the need for dental surgery.

The treatment, called silver diamine fluoride (SDF), takes only seconds to apply to each affected tooth. Rather than removing damaged tooth material and placing a filling, a dentist uses a tiny sponge tipped applicator to paint the liquid directly onto the cavity. The process requires no drilling, injections, or sedation.

The findings could have enormous implications for childhood dental care. Every year, thousands of young children in the United States visit emergency departments because of untreated cavities. Emergency physicians generally cannot provide the dental procedures needed to address the underlying problem, leaving some children with ongoing pain and infections. Others ultimately need dental surgery under general anesthesia, which makes them completely unconscious during the procedure.
Now, researchers led by the University of Michigan have produced compelling evidence that a much simpler approach can stop many cavities from getting worse.
Major Clinical Trial Confirms Silver Diamine Fluoride Works

Published in JAMA Pediatrics, the Phase III clinical trial included 830 children younger than 6. Participants were recruited through dental clinics, pediatric medical practices, and Head Start and Early Head Start programs in Michigan, New York, and Iowa.
Head Start and Early Head Start are federally supported programs that provide early childhood education and related services to eligible families.
The results showed that a solution containing 38% silver diamine fluoride successfully stopped decay in more than half of the affected baby teeth when treatment was provided at six month intervals.

Dentists refer to this as arresting tooth decay, meaning the damaged area stops deteriorating. Unlike a traditional filling, the treatment does not replace lost tooth structure. Instead, it helps prevent existing decay from progressing.

SDF works through the combined effects of silver and fluoride. Silver helps combat bacteria associated with tooth decay, while fluoride helps strengthen the mineral structure of teeth and resist further damage.

"This is a very effective and safe treatment -- even in children as young as 1," said Margherita Fontana, professor of dentistry at the University of Michigan School of Dentistry and the study's lead investigator.
A Simple Treatment Could Help Millions Avoid Dental Pain

Tooth decay is the most common chronic disease among children, affecting more than 40% of American children. Although cavities may initially cause few noticeable symptoms, untreated decay can eventually lead to severe toothaches, infections, problems eating and sleeping, missed school days, and repeated medical appointments.
For young children, conventional dental treatment can also be particularly challenging. Some are too young to remain still throughout a procedure, while others experience significant fear or anxiety.
SDF offers an alternative for many of these patients because it can be applied quickly without the equipment and procedures required for a traditional filling.

Fontana said the benefits could extend well beyond young children. Older adults, people with developmental or physical disabilities, individuals with severe dental anxiety, and patients who have difficulty obtaining conventional dental care could also benefit.

There is, however, one important tradeoff. SDF permanently turns the decayed portion of a treated tooth dark, which can be especially noticeable on front teeth. The discoloration is primarily cosmetic, but it may influence whether patients and families choose the treatment.
For many people, avoiding pain, drilling, or more invasive procedures may outweigh that drawback.
Why This Decades-Old Treatment Could Soon Reach More Patients
Silver diamine fluoride is not a newly invented substance. Dentists have successfully used it to manage cavities in numerous countries for decades.

In the United States, the FDA approved SDF as a medical device for treating tooth sensitivity in 2014. Dentists have also used it off-label to stop cavities, meaning they apply an authorized product for a purpose beyond its original approved indication.

What has been missing is large-scale clinical evidence from U.S. populations establishing its safety and effectiveness for treating tooth decay, a key step toward obtaining FDA approval for that specific use.
The University of Michigan trial was designed to help fill that gap.

"If we want more children and families to benefit from this treatment, we need rigorous evidence showing both that it works and that it's safe. From a public health perspective, if we want broader implementation across the United States, including in medical settings, we need carefully collected data in U.S. populations, and we now have that," Fontana said.
The investigation began in 2018 and continued despite the major disruptions caused by the COVID-19 pandemic.

The researchers believe stronger clinical evidence could make SDF more widely available, including in pediatric medical settings where children often receive care long before their first dental appointment.

"In medicine, clinicians want high-quality evidence before changing practice," Fontana said. "It is important to have data they can refer to because young children often see pediatricians years before they ever visit a dentist, broader acceptance could allow many more cavities to be treated while a referral to a dental home is successful, and before they become painful, infected or require surgery."
A dental home refers to an ongoing relationship with a dental care provider who can deliver preventive care, treatment, and follow-up services.
Expanding access to SDF could allow more children to receive early intervention before relatively manageable cavities develop into serious dental problems.
FDA Approval Could Expand Access to Cavity Treatment

The trial brought together researchers from the University of Michigan, New York University, the University of Iowa, and Indiana University. The National Institute of Dental and Craniofacial Research, part of the National Institutes of Health, provided more than $12 million in funding.
The product tested was Advantage Arrest 38% SDF, supplied by Elevate Oral Care.
The findings provide clinical trial evidence that the manufacturer can use in an application seeking FDA approval of SDF as a drug for arresting dental caries, the medical term for tooth decay.
Amr Moursi, a professor of pediatric dentistry at New York University College of Dentistry and a co-principal investigator, emphasized the potential importance of that regulatory change.

"Our results support FDA approval of SDF for managing arrest of tooth decay in young children. Removing SDF from off-label status would be an important innovation which could lead to increased utilization by providers, enhanced payments by insurers and more consistent product quality," said Moursi, a co-principal investigator on the study.
For some children, receiving another application of SDF every few months could be sufficient to keep a cavity under control until the affected baby tooth naturally falls out.
Adults could also benefit, either by using SDF to manage decay over a longer period or as a temporary solution until a filling or another restorative procedure becomes affordable or practical.

The treatment is not suitable for every cavity, and stopping decay does not necessarily eliminate the need for future dental work. Nevertheless, the findings suggest that a procedure requiring only seconds to perform could help many patients avoid more complicated treatment.
"For almost anyone, this can arrest the decay and stop the infection and the pain it causes," Fontana said. "This could benefit many people."
Materials provided by University of Michigan. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

- Margherita Fontana, Amr Moursi, Carlos Gonzalez-Cabezas, Divya Khera, Steven M. Levy, George J. Eckert, Barry P. Katz, Livia M. A. Tenuta, Marcia S. Campos, Elisabeta Karl, James Boynton, Courtney Chinn, Alex Sheen, Justine Kolker, John Warren, Emily Thorpe. Efficacy of Silver Diamine Fluoride on Young Children With Severe Early Childhood Caries. JAMA Pediatrics, 2026; 180 (9): 942 DOI: 10.1001/jamapediatrics.2026.2567

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 23, 2007: NASA launches Harmony module to ISS on STS-120 space shuttle mission
articles.author: Hanneke Weitering

paras.en: On October 23, 2007, the space shuttle Discovery launched the Harmony module to the International Space Station.

The Harmony module is a utility hub 14 feet wide and 24 feet long, or about the length of a minibus. It joins the European Space Agency's Columbus module and Japan's Kibo laboratory and serves as the crew quarters for the American astronauts.

Once it was installed, the space station grew from about the size of a three-bedroom house to something more like a five-bedroom house. When astronauts delivered Harmony to the space station, they left it temporarily attached to the Unity node.

After the shuttle left, astronauts used the space station's robotic arm to move the shuttle docking port out of the way at the Destiny module. This made room for Harmony to then dock at its permanent home next to the Destiny module.
In 2007, the International Space Station was much smaller than it is today in terms of living space for its astronaut crew. The Harmony connecting module changed all that.

The STS-120 mission opened a new phase of ISS expansion by adding a vital connecting hub for future modules. Prior to Harmony's launch, the last new room addition to the ISS had occurred in 2001, when Russia's Pirs docking module (since discarded) arrived.

The Harmony module (its original name was Node 2), was the second NASA-led hub module (after the Unity, or Node 1, module) for the ISS. It was built for NASA by the Italy-based Thales Alenia Space and is covered with five "common berthing mechanisms," or connecting points for different ISS modules.

After the two-week STS-120 flight, Harmony was moved from a temporary berth at the Unity module to the forward port on the NASA's main Destiny laboratory. Once there, it served as a connection point for Europe's Columbus lab on the starboard side, and Japan's massive Kibo lab on the port side. Some of its ports have been used by visiting caargo ships and a docking port on its roof allows visiting vehicles to park there.

Inside the module are eight payload racks that include four used for avionics and four others for either stowage or crew quarters. NASA's astronaut crew quarters are based in the Harmony module. The name Harmony was selected durng a public naming contest by NASA.
Want more space history? Check out our full On This Day In Space Story archive and watch our On This Day In Space videos on YouTube.

Hanneke Weitering is a multimedia journalist in the Pacific Northwest reporting on the future of aviation at FutureFlight.aero and Aviation International News and was previously the Editor for Spaceflight and Astronomy news here at Space.com. As an editor with over 10 years of experience in science journalism she has previously written for Scholastic Classroom Magazines, MedPage Today and The Joint Institute for Computational Sciences at Oak Ridge National Laboratory. After studying physics at the University of Tennessee in her hometown of Knoxville, she earned her graduate degree in Science, Health and Environmental Reporting (SHERP) from New York University. Hanneke joined the Space.com team in 2016 as a staff writer and producer, covering topics including spaceflight and astronomy. She currently lives in Seattle, home of the Space Needle, with her cat and two snakes. In her spare time, Hanneke enjoys exploring the Rocky Mountains, basking in nature and looking for dark skies to gaze at the cosmos.

articles.title: NASA lays out plan for Artemis 3 moon-lander test flight —but when will it launch?
articles.author: Mike Wall

paras.en: NASA just gave us our best look yet at its Artemis III moon-lander test flight.

The agency laid out a detailed concept of operations for Artemis III today (Oct. 23) during a press conference at Kennedy Space Center, stressing how important the flight is to its moon plans and how challenging it will be to make everything go right.

"We're launching three of the most powerful rockets in the world, and undertaking what is likely the most complicated launch campaign ever undertaken," Jeremy Parsons, NASA’s Artemis program manager, said during today's event, which lasted more than two hours.
Those three rockets are NASA's Space Launch System (SLS), SpaceX's Starship and Blue Origin's New Glenn, all of which will fly from Florida's Space Coast.

If all goes according to plan, New Glenn will lift off first, carrying Blue Origin's Blue Moon lunar lander to low Earth orbit (LEO). SLS will go next, launching the Artemis III astronauts — NASA's Randy Bresnik, Andre Douglas and Frank Rubio, and the European Space Agency's Luca Parmitano — aboard NASA's Orion spacecraft.

SLS will deploy Orion into a highly elliptical orbit, one that gets as close to Earth as 18 miles (29 kilometers) and as far away as 1,122 miles (1,806 km), according to Parsons. The capsule will then maneuver itself into an orbit with an altitude of about 345 miles (555 km).

"That's really about getting thermal stability," Parsons said. "Orion was built as a deep-space vehicle, and so we're going to have to really manage the thermal environments, which are higher in a low Earth orbit."
The Artemis III crew will spend two days checking out Orion and its systems in LEO before meeting up with Blue Moon, which will take place on Flight Day 3 at an altitude of 273 miles (439 km).

"Over the next two days, the crew will conduct operations docked with Blue Moon," Parsons said. "They're going to open up the hatch. They're going to enter the lander. They're going to evaluate the environmental controls, the life support systems. We'll confirm that the spacecraft can maintain the right atmospheric pressure, and we're also going to test emergency scenarios, dual vehicle control, and we're going to put our Mission Control teams through their paces."
After those operations are complete — likely on Flight Day 6 or thereabouts — Starship will launch, with a specially built docking adapter on its nose.

The SpaceX vehicle — the 171-foot-tall (52 meters) upper stage of its fully reusable Starship megarocket — will meet up with Orion in LEO on Flight Day 8, at an altitude of about 237 miles (381 km). But this will be a very different encounter than the rendezvous with Blue Moon.

"The demonstration with Starship is shorter, about two hours," Parsons said. "The crew will not enter the Starship during the mission, but it gives us critical data and allows us to really understand the forces of docking, how we're going to push, how we're going to work together."

Artemis III will continue for another six to nine days after Orion undocks from Starship before finally heading back down to Earth for a parachute-aided ocean splashdown. (The nominal mission length is 14 days, Parsons said, but it could last as long as 17 days.)

During that time, the crew will evaluate their survival suits — something that didn't get done during the 10-day Artemis II flight around the moon this past April — and do a variety of other work as well, from detailed health assessments to scientific experiments and technology demonstrations. The main goal is to keep everything on track for Artemis IV, which will land astronauts near the moon's south pole in 2028, if all goes to plan.

"Everything we do on Artemis III is designed to reduce risk for our future lunar landing missions," Parsons said. "We're teaching these teams how to work together, how to make critical real-time mission decisions, all in an environment that is low Earth orbit, where if something goes wrong, we can come home much more quickly."
It's unclear at the moment which of these two privately developed landers — Blue Moon or Starship — will fly on Artemis IV, pulling off the first crewed lunar touchdown since Apollo 17 in 1972.

NASA is still preserving optionality, "to give both of our lunar landing partners the greatest opportunity for readiness in advance of astronauts landing on the moon in 2028," NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said during today's event.
"We have no intention of surrendering a viable path to the surface before the data and schedule compels us to do so," he added.

No matter what decision NASA makes for Artemis IV, both Blue Moon and Starship should hit the gray dirt relatively soon, according to Parsons. "Regardless of who goes first, both providers are planning for lunar landing missions in 2028," he said.

And those missions will be quite different from each other. For example, on Blue Origin touchdowns, Orion will meet up with Blue Moon in lunar orbit. On SpaceX landings, however, Starship will likely dock with the NASA capsule in Earth orbit and propel it to the moon, Parsons said — the "push" he referred to above.

It remains unclear when exactly Artemis III will launch. NASA is targeting the summer of next year but may find it tough to meet that timeline: Last month, in an internal memo, Isaacman told agency employees that Artemis III was about 90 days behind schedule.

Some of the biggest challenges have involved the supply chain for the mission's lunar landers, Parsons said during today's event. But he and Isaacman both stressed that NASA is confident in its ability to work through such issues.
"We're moving with real speed and purpose right now," Isaacman said.

Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. He primarily covers human and robotic spaceflight, military space, and exoplanets, but has been known to dabble in the space art beat. His book about the search for alien life, "Out There," was published on Nov. 13, 2018. Before becoming a science writer, Michael worked as a herpetologist and wildlife biologist. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. To find out what his latest project is, you can follow Michael on Twitter.

articles.title: SpaceX launches Starlink satellites from California as Falcon 9 cadence slows (video)
articles.author: Josh Dinner

paras.en: SpaceX launched its newest batch of Starlink broadband internet satellites today (Oct. 23) from the California coast.

The spacecraft, Starlink Group 15-15, were stacked 27 high inside the payload fairing of a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket, which lifted off from Pad 4E at Vandenberg Space Force Base at 6:48 p.m. EDT (2248 GMT; 3:48 p.m. local time in California).

The rocket's first stage booster, designated B1063, executed its main engine cutoff and stage separation about 2.5 minutes into flight, sending the second stage to continue onward to low Earth orbit (LEO). The vehicle's two-piece protective payload fairing was jettisoned just before T+3 minutes.

The booster, meanwhile, reoriented for its descent back to Earth. As the mission clock passed 8 minutes, B1063 began its landing burn, and it touched down about 20 seconds later on SpaceX's droneship "Of Course I Still Love You." This was the 36th launch and landing for B1063, which notably launched NASA's DART asteroid-smashing mission in November 2021.

The Falcon 9's upper stage completed its first engine burn shortly after B1063 landed and will coast for about 45 minutes before initiating a second and final orbital insertion burn. Following that burn's execution, deployment of the vehicle's 27 satellites into LEO is scheduled to begin 62 minutes after launch.

Today's Starlink liftoff adds to SpaceX's growing constellation of more than 11,000 active spacecraft. But Starlinks aren't launching quite as often as they used to, as SpaceX shifts its focus from the Falcon 9 to its bigger and more powerful Starship rocket.

Starship is designed for full reusability and is equipped with a payload bay outfitted to accommodate SpaceX's upgraded Version 3 Starlink satellites, which are too large for the workhorse Falcon 9. Starship is still under development, but once the rocket begins operational flights (and that day is getting closer), SpaceX plans to phase out the Falcon 9 and its Falcon Heavy variant almost entirely.

Falcon 9's 100th launch of 2026 was the Starlink 10-49 group from SpaceX's pad at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, which was later revealed to be the final Falcon 9 Starlink mission that would fly from Florida's Space Coast. The same might soon be true for Starlink launches from the West Coast as well.

The reduction in missions lifting off from Florida has slowed Falcon 9's Starlink launch cadence considerably. At their peak, these missions were flying every two to three days. But the most recent one before today lifted off 11 days ago, and that launch itself was the first Starlink mission in more than three weeks.

Today's launch was the 116th Falcon 9 flight so far in 2026, with about three-quarters of those being dedicated to Starlink. The reduced cadence will likely solidify 2025 as the Falcon 9's busiest year ever, with 165 launches completed. At its current rate, the Falcon 9 is expected to fly just under 150 missions by the end of this year.

Josh Dinner is Space.com's Spaceflight Staff Writer and a photographer with a passion for science and space exploration. He has worked the space beat since 2016, covering the evolution of NASA's commercial spaceflight partnerships and crewed missions from the Space Coast, planetary science missions, the Artemis program and humanity's return to the moon and more. He also enjoys building 1:144-scale model rockets and spacecraft. Find some of Josh's launch photography on Instagram, and follow him on X, where he mostly posts in haiku.

articles.title: Jena-Optronik is proud to partner with MDA Space for its first ASTRO HP mission.
articles.author: Jena-Optronik

paras.en: MDA Space, a global leader in communications satellites, Earth and space observation, space exploration and infrastructure, will utilize Jena-Optronik’s ASTRO HP star sensor on a LEO mission. This milestone underscores our ability to provide cutting-edge technology that meets the demands of international space missions.

In a market that moves fast, the ASTRO HP optical head provides the perfect balance: high performance thanks to the radiation-hard Faintstar2 detector, the very fast optics in a compact, lightweight design optimized for small and medium-sized, high-performance satellites.

articles.title: ‘Burden and loss’ builds in DR Congo, as Kenya strengthens Ebola containment

paras.en: ‘Burden and loss’ builds in DR Congo, as Kenya strengthens Ebola containment

“If we lift the foot off the pedal, the virus will resurge very quickly, will continue to spread to newly affected areas and pose a threat for the country, the region and the world at large,” warned Dr. Catherine Smallwood, World Health Organization (WHO) incident manager in the DRC.

The country remains the epicentre of an outbreak of Ebola Bundibugyo virus disease that was officially declared in mid-May. It began in the volatile eastern region and has now spread to eight provinces, the latest being Nord-Ubangi in the northwest.
There have been 9,765 cases to date and nearly half – 4,727 – have died. Additionally, 30,000 contacts are being monitored each day over a three-week period.
A smaller outbreak in Uganda was officially declared over in August, while cases have also been confirmed in Kenya, Nigeria and France.

In the DRC, “we’re seeing an incredible permanent burden and loss of livelihoods in those families that are affected”, said Dr. Smallwood, speaking from the eastern city of Bunia to journalists in Geneva.

At nearly six months in, the outbreak “is occurring in an area that is geographically vast and moving into ever hard to reach locations and remote locations”, she noted. Some places can take several days to reach by boat or motorcycle and are inaccessible by car or plane.

The crisis continues to unfold amid ongoing conflict, hunger and displacement, and the World Food Programme (WFP) is working to ensure that families get enough to eat. The UN agency is also building Ebola treatment centres, among other operations.
WFP’s Representative in the DRC David Stevenson shared stories of the people who depend on its support.
One woman, Francine Birungi Amoti, lost a child to Ebola and is raising her six surviving children and a baby entrusted to her care. She is unable to attend to her fields due to violence.
“For Francine, food assistance means being able to feed the children in her care when reaching her fields could cost her life,” he said, speaking from the capital Kinshasa.
“This is what a crisis on top of a crisis looks like: disease and bereavement, compounded by insecurity and hunger.”
Dr. Smallwood also pointed to another concern as the number of people dying from Ebola outside recognised treatment centres “remains a big flag of late detection of cases at the community level”.

The past week has seen a decline in the number of people dying in the community or outside Ebola treatment centres which indicates that actions to increase early detection and quick referral to care have been working.

However, WHO understands that in some parts of eastern DRC, “patients are visiting between two to five different health facilities before they're referred to Ebola treatment centres”, representing “a really, really big challenge”.

Dr. Smallwood said there have been significant improvements in the quality of care provided at Ebola treatment centres. WHO had set a target of 3,000 beds across affected areas and currently over 2,000 are available.

She also highlighted the positive fact that 2,600 people in the DRC have survived Ebola. Clinics are being opened where they can access care, including to monitor presence of the virus and any related conditions that may arise, as well as psychosocial support.

There is also good news on the Ebola front in Kenya following the country’s first case and fatality earlier this month – a Kenyan man who had been working in the DRC before flying back to Nairobi via Uganda.
More than 100 contacts were identified, some of whom will complete their 21-day quarantine on Sunday and will be heading home to their families.
WHO representative in Kenya Dr. Neema Rusibamayila Kimambo welcomed the development.
“I think their sacrifice has been important in ensuring that the community is protected and that we don’t have community spread today,” she told UN News.
She stressed that these people should not be stigmatised as being released from quarantine does not mean that they had Ebola, only that they had contact with someone who did.
With Ebola now confirmed in four African countries, Dr. Kimambo underscored that governments must remain vigilant.

“Africa is very interconnected and nobody is safe until everyone is safe,” she said. “So, as long as we have Ebola in DRC at the scale that it is, or in any other country, it means that we are not safe. Therefore, the key message is preparedness.”

articles.title: Soil mapping aims to boost agricultural production in Kenya

paras.en: Soil mapping aims to boost agricultural production in Kenya

The Soil Mapping for Resilient Agrifood systems (SoilFER) programme supports farmers to develop reliable soil information that will inform agricultural decisions such as which fertilizer to use and how much.

So far, more than 3,600 soil samples have been collected and mapped across 45 counties, contributing to a digital soil map designed to provide farmers with location-specific information about their land.
Select farmers also receive training to diagnose and fix soil degradation – earning the title “soil doctor” – who then go on to teach their peers.

SoilFER was launched through a partnership between the UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) and the Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organization (KALRO) in Kabete, with financial support from the United States Department of State and Japan.
For Agness Munialo, a farmer from Kakamega county in western Kenya, learning about soil composition and fertility has changed how she thinks about farming.
“Farmers would use excessive chemicals, sometimes even more fertilizers in an attempt to get more yields. Now we know better,” she said.

Ms. Munialo, a trained soil doctor who participated in the SoilFER programme, said the initiative was helping farmers, particularly in rural areas, better understand soil composition, pH levels and fertility.
According to Barrack Okoba, FAO-Kenya’s national coordinator of the programme, making soil information accessible is essential to building resilience in agriculture.
“Part of resilience is to make sure that our information system is available and supporting farmers to build sustainable farm management,” he said.
Through the support of FAO, KALRO has renovated three labs and equipped them with state-of-the-art technology to support analysis of soil samples collected across the country.
The samples are georeferenced, with the findings transmitted directly to farmers’ mobile phones.
The initiative is also attracting interest from young people exploring opportunities in agriculture.
Jackline Kioko, a KALRO intern who participated in the launch, said the information shared had given her a better understanding of how soil testing could inform decisions on her family’s farm.
“I'd love to do farming more, now that I have the information that you can actually test your soils to know what nutrients it requires,” she said.

Kenya’s Cabinet Secretary for Agriculture, Mutahi Kagwe called for stronger collaboration among agricultural institutions to promote coordinated decision-making, enhance information sharing, and ensure that soil health is integrated into the work of all relevant institutions.
“I want to urge Kenyans that before thinking about what to plant or the fertilizer to use, think about soil testing,” he said.
The event also marked the launch of the Kenya Soil Partnership, the Kenya Soil Laboratory Network and the national rollout of the Global Soil Doctors Programme.
The SoilFER programme is currently being implemented in six other countries: Ghana, Guatemala, Honduras, Mozambique, Tunisia and Zambia.

articles.title: Why do planes keep circling before landing? The UN has a plan to fix it

paras.en: Why do planes keep circling before landing? The UN has a plan to fix it

Air traffic delays cost billions and turn journeys into ordeals. Some countries are already proving that better coordination saves thousands of flying hours and cuts emissions – and the UN’s aviation agency wants the rest of the world to follow.
Most frequent flyers know the feeling: the plane begins its descent but, instead of heading for the runway, starts circling overhead.
It isn’t necessarily a fault or bad weather. Often, it is a holding pattern – a manoeuvre that keeps aircraft airborne until there is room for them to land.
It is one symptom of increasingly crowded skies, where a storm, an emergency or a closed route in one place can cause delays thousands of kilometres away.
The bill is enormous. In Europe alone, air traffic management delays cost an estimated $2.3 billion or more in 2025, according to EUROCONTROL, the continent’s air navigation body.
What if countries coordinated their flights the way a city synchronises its traffic lights?
That is the idea behind a push by the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO), the UN agency that sets global aviation standards.
“If the traffic lights work independently, traffic becomes chaos and there are jams on every corner,” ICAO Secretary General Juan Carlos Salazar told UN News.
“If you get a green light on one street and are stopped at the next, the backlog builds immediately. The same happens with air traffic across the world’s airspace.”

The fix starts long before landing. If an airport knows it cannot take more aircraft for a while, it can coordinate with other airports to hold back departures, rather than leave planes circling overhead.
This approach, known as air traffic flow management, lets airlines, airports, controllers and weather services share information and make decisions together.

Several countries already use it, but the benefits are limited when national systems don’t talk to each other. After five days of talks in Montreal convened by ICAO, governments and industry backed a faster global rollout.
For passengers, that should mean earlier warning of cancellations and delays as well as quicker recovery when things go wrong.
“When people get to the airport, wait all day and nobody tells them anything, that creates huge problems,” Mr. Salazar said.
Disruption snowballs, he explained. A problem lasting an hour or a day knocks on to every flight scheduled after it and today’s system is slow to bounce back.
The gains are already measurable. In the Americas, collaborative trials supported by ICAO saved more than 265,000 minutes of flying time in 2026, about 4,400 hours, and over $38.9 million.
They also saved some 13,330 tonnes of fuel and avoided 42,160 tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions, a contribution to the goal of net zero carbon emissions from international aviation by 2050.

In Europe, a EUROCONTROL programme anticipating weather and congestion avoided around 3.1 million minutes of delay between May and August 2026, saving an estimated $448 million and making the network 14 per cent more stable on the worst days.
Brazil and Colombia have run such systems for years, Mr. Salazar said, but largely at national level while international flights cross many countries’ airspace.
“Technology alone is not the answer,” he said. Information has to be shared and often it isn’t, sometimes for lack of will, sometimes for lack of the means to transmit it in real time.

“A flight from Europe to Australia or New Zealand passes through four or five regions, different continents and that requires excellent coordination which doesn’t exist today,” he said. “No country or region acting alone can manage that.”

ICAO, with 193 member States, sets common standards and provides technical help so countries can coordinate regardless of resources. New international rules on flow management are due in November 2030, with regional workshops planned for 2027.
The pressure is mounting. ICAO projects air travel could reach 12.4 billion passengers by 2050.

Other challenges are piling up. Conflicts force airlines to reroute around danger zones, creating new bottlenecks. Drones, air taxis, rocket launches and unplanned re-entries of objects from orbit all demand closer coordination.
For Mr. Salazar, the goal is simple: “an air transport system that reaches every person in the world, so that everyone sees the benefits of being connected.”

articles.title: Mbappe's late strike earns Mourinho and Real Clasico glory at Barca

paras.en: Barcelona vs Real Madrid; Spanish La Liga
Barcelona vs Real Madrid. Spanish La Liga.
Barcelona 1-2 Real Madrid: Kylian Mbappe scores late winner in El Clasico to beat LaLiga leaders

Match report as Kylian Mbappe grabs late winner for Real Madrid in thrilling El Clasico at Spotify Camp Nou; Barcelona equalised through Raphinha after Mbappe deflected in opener but Jude Bellingham brilliance set Real away to grab three LaLiga points and close in on rivals
Kylian Mbappe's double took Real Madrid to a famous 2-1 Clasico win, which had Jose Mourinho sliding on his knees in celebration in Barcelona.

It was the 87th minute when Mbappe tucked in from Eduardo Camavinga's cutback following some sublime skill from Jude Bellingham. The celebrations from Real Madrid were wild, with their head coach unable to contain himself, his staff on the pitch, and his players clashing with Barcelona fans.

Real had been on the defensive after Raphinha's snapshot had levelled a pulsating clash, with Lamine Yamal narrowly clipping wide as LaLiga's defending champions pushed for a winner. Instead Real have closed to within three points of their great rivals. Atletico are second just two off Barca now.

It's been a bad week for Hansi Flick's side, whose 11-game winning streak at the start of this season was halted with defeat in the Champions League at Paris St-Germain. This loss will sting far more - it's Real's first win in Barcelona in three years.

Mbappe's opener had been fortuitous, Gerard Martin slamming a clearance in off him. But Real's move to get to that point had been excellent and throughout the contest they showed they were willing to go toe-to-toe with their more favoured hosts.
There was controversy before Raphinha's equaliser, with Joao Cancelo not punished for putting his studs into Yan Diomande's calf. But Mourinho and Real Madrid will leave Spotify Camp Nou celebrating.
18: SHOT! It's end-to-end as Guler steps in off the right and forces Garcia into a save moments after Gordon tested Lunin.
24: SHOTS! Raphinha whacks one over the bar from 16 yards and then links up brilliantly with Gordon before bending a low effort just wide.
33: OVER! Mbappe scissor-kicks over the bar after a brilliant move featuring a big Bellingham tackle and Guler's gorgeous cross.
41: GOAL! Mbappe gives Real the lead when Gerard Martin whacks the ball against him from Diomande's cross into the box! A bizarre goal at the end of a fine team move from the visitors.
50: CHANCE! But Bellingham can't find the pass to Mbappe after skipping away on the counter to set up a two-on-one against Martin, who shuts him down.
57: CONTROVERSY! Cancelo puts his studs into Diomande's calf. The Real winger continues his attack before going to ground - but there's no retrospective punishment for the Barca defender.
61: GOAL! Pedri reverses a pass into Raphinha and his snapshot beats Lunin, who got a hand to the ball but couldn't keep the equaliser out.
66: SAVE! An amazing save from Lunin, as he claws away Martin's powerful header from a corner.
78: CLOSE! Lamine Yamal skips past a couple of challenges then clips a shot at goal - but the ball bounces just wide.
87: GOAL! Mbappe sensationally wins it for Real, slotting in after Camavinga cuts the ball back to him following sublime skill from Bellingham.

articles.title: Smith beats Schindler in Dortmund thriller after Littler's QF exit

paras.en: European Championship Darts: Ross Smith beats Martin Schindler to Dortmund title after Luke Littler's quarter-final exit

Luke Littler suffered a quarter-final exit to Krzysztof Ratajski, extending his wait for his elusive ranked TV title; Ross Smith beat Martin Schindler in the European Championship final; Watch the Grand Slam of Darts in Wolverhampton live on Sky Sports from November 14-22
Ross Smith has won the Machineseeker European Championship for a second time after overcoming a late Martin Schindler fightback to claim an 11-8 victory in Dortmund.

The 2022 champion fired a 107 average in his last-eight victory over Luke Woodhouse and rallied from 4-1 down to beat Gerwyn Price 11-7, setting up a showdown against German No 1 Schindler at Westfalenhallen.
Smith edged a tight opening session before reeling off six straight legs against Schindler, who almost fell 9-2 behind before capitalising on some wayward finishing to sneak a 20-dart break of throw.

Schindler was broken in the next but offered a four-leg burst - including finishes of 116 and 127 - to cut the deficit to 9-7 and threaten a famous comeback, but the next three legs went with throw as Smith closed out victory and the £150,000 first prize.

Victory sees Smith join Michael van Gerwen, Phil Taylor, Rob Cross and Peter Wright as the only players to win multiple European Championship titles, with his latest success following his World Series of Darts title in September and lifting him to world No 6.

"I'm not going to lie, I was a bit sweaty there going to that end with Martin - he wouldn't let up, would he!" Smith said. "Full credit to him. To have this trophy in my hands, to win another major - I'm absolutely over the moon and drained, but I'm buzzing!"
Luke Littler was the pre-tournament favourite to claim the only missing ranked major from his glittering CV, only for the world No 1 to suffer a shock quarter-final exit to Krzysztof Ratajaski.

Schindler thrashed Jonny Clayton 10-1 and despatched Ratajaski - who eliminated Littler 11-6 in the previous round - to reach his maiden ranked TV final, with the German missing chances to grab the early lead against Smith.
He wasted multiple opportunities to break in the third leg but responded with a 14-dart hold in the next, levelling the match, before Smith quickly pulled away.

Smith took out an 86 finish to break and kept the German crowd quiet by sweeping all five legs in the next mini session, with Schindler only allowed back in when his opponent squandered five darts at double to open a seven-leg lead.

The pair traded breaks of throw before Schindler followed a 15-dart hold by firing successive ton-plus checkouts, with Smith stuttering over the closing legs before wrapping up victory with his fifth match dart.

"It's a strange one. I really don't think I played great this week," Smith added. "I think a lot of players let me off as well, but sometimes you have to win ugly. I'm proud of doing that because you have got to dig deep. You have to really fight hard and I think I've done that this weekend."
Despite just falling short of a first Premier title, Schindler made history in reaching the European Championship final on home soil and becoming the first German to reach a televised final.
"When I started playing darts ten years ago, I didn't expect anything and now I made a major final," said an emotional Schindler.
"I tried everything to win this one, but fair play to Ross, he played well. I lost but I'm still very happy! I'm going to be in the Grand Slam now. That's probably the best part of it!

articles.title: 'The pace was rubbish' - Russell in blunt admission after Austin struggle

paras.en: George Russell: Mercedes driver admits to 'rubbish' pace in United States GP after finishing almost one minute behind Kimi Antonelli

Mercedes driver finished seven places and 54 seconds behind dominant race-winning team-mate Kimi Antonelli after struggle in the W17 car; Antonelli poised to clinch the world championship this weekend in Mexico after growing lead over Russell to 123 points
George Russell admitted his pace in the United States Grand Prix was "rubbish", with the Mercedes driver at a loss to why he trailed race-winning team-mate Kimi Antonelli by such a large margin,

Russell finished 54 seconds behind the sister Mercedes in the 56-lap race in an eighth place that only just kept him in mathematical championship contention heading to this week's race in Mexico, where Antonelli is set to clinch the crown.

Russell had held his grid position of sixth through the race's first stint but dropped to eighth after serving a five-second penalty at his sole pit stop for an incident with Oscar Piastri in the opening lap, when he was judged to have gained an advantage over the McLaren by running off track and retaining position.

Russell subsequently spent the final 26 laps on the similarly one-stopping Piastri's tail but was unable to find a way back past the Australian driver.
Russell told Sky Sports F1: "The pace was rubbish. That's the long and short of it.
"The five-second [penalty] didn't help things and probably cost me two or three positions but the pace wasn't good enough when it needed to be."
Russell made no excuse for his lack of competitiveness and said he had no immediate answer for why his Austin weekend was such a struggle.
"I need to try and understand why that is. It's strange when you're so far off.
"Hopefully there are some answers somewhere but at the moment I don't have them."
Antonelli's win was his ninth of the year and represented what Toto Wolff, Mercedes' team principal, believes was "the best race that he's delivered so far".

It was the first win for Mercedes upgraded car, which has taken time for the world championship leaders to get the best out of since the aerodynamic revisions debuted at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia at the start of October.
The team have said, however, that the changes have narrowed the car's optimum set-up window.
On Russell's weekend, Wolff said: "George just struggled so much. And I believe this is because the operational window of the car is so difficult.
"In Q2 he was there and thereabouts. Q3, it didn't work. He said, 'that goes on me'.

"And today in the race, I don't know, we got stuck behind Piastri, which looks a bit unfair why he didn't get past. It's the same engine, it's the same electric charging and deployment. But I'm going to see him now."
'He's not 54 seconds slower over a race distance'
Analysis from Sky Sports F1's Jenson Button:

"George has had a lot of tough races but also some great races and that's the thing that's really difficult to understand - how he's able to get the maximum out of that car on some tracks but not at others.

"Austin was difficult as he started so far down. He was in the pack and when you're in the pack, sometimes it's difficult to move forward. You're in the dirty air. You try to do something different with strategy but then you get a five-second penalty which puts you back further.
"I don't believe his pace is that far off. He's not 54 seconds slower over a race distance."

articles.title: NFL fans visiting Paris in high spirits for Saints vs. Steelers game, undeterred by protests
articles.author: Doha Madani

paras.en: PARIS — American football fans brought high energy, chants and smiles to Stade de France on Sunday to watch the Pittsburgh Steelers face the New Orleans Saints. Some said the mass protests in the city were not an issue during their weekend trip.

The NFL’s first regular-season game in France came a day after more than 400,000 people around the country took to the streets to protest educational funding and the high cost of living. At least 110,000 of those protesters were concentrated in Paris, according to the French Interior Ministry.

Although the demonstrations were largely peaceful, some clashes broke out, prompting French security forces to use tear gas and water cannons in several cities. Paris prosecutors said there were 64 arrests in the nation’s capital on Saturday, mostly for suspected weapons offenses or participation in a group preparing violence or property damage.
But American visitors in town to cheer on their teams told NBC News that everyone they’ve encountered had been welcoming.

Lifelong friends and Saints fans Sindhu Pandit, Shruti Menon and Pramod Menon said they never felt the game would be canceled. Pandit said the key to their own movements around the city was to stay informed.

Pramod Menon added that locals were “incredibly hospitable” and considerate of the fact that they were visitors. The friends said they came to support both the country and their team, a sentiment his wife shared.
“We’re so excited to be here in Paris, and what a perfect place for New Orleans, the home of the French,” Shruti Menon said. “And so it’s wonderful to be here.”
Sean Warner, a Steelers fan since 1974, may not share the Menons’ taste in teams, but he also told NBC News that he and his wife, Saroja, were having a “wonderful” time in Paris.

“We were concerned about the riots and everything that we had heard about and read about, but quite honestly, it’s been amazing,” he said. “The experience has been fantastic. ... Paris has really tried to work hard to, you know, make people feel safe and comfortable, and then enjoy the experience.”

The Washington, D.C.-based couple, who have visited Paris several times, spent Saturday walking around the city. Saroja Warner said it was a bit sad to see some businesses with boarded-up windows, but any clashes seemed “localized.”

“We walked around Paris all day till about 6 o’clock at night ... and we didn’t see any unrest, any crazy stuff,” she said. “It just felt like a lot of folks trying to have a nice time on a rainy day in Paris.”

The Steelers beat the Saints 16-10 at France’s national stadium, just outside the heart of Paris. The game is the latest in a series of international games the NFL has scheduled in recent seasons to grow the sport outside of its domestic audience.

NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell told reporters Wednesday that he was not concerned about the Paris protests ahead of the game and was comfortable with the security preparations the league had made in coordination with French authorities.
“Protests are not unusual in France, as you know, and that’s something that we will be aware of and make sure that the appropriate arrangements are made,” Goodell said.

Figures from the Interior Ministry indicate Saturday’s demonstrations produced significantly fewer problems than those the week before. There were about 1,300 arrests nationwide, roughly half the previous week’s total. Only 53 members of the security forces reported injuries, compared with 1,144 the week before, according to the ministry.

The unrest began weeks ago, when students at a high school in Créteil, a suburb of Paris, began protesting a lack of resources and poor conditions at their school. Students at other schools in the poorer suburbs surrounding Paris soon joined, and the protests grew into a movement of students across France.

The teenagers blocked entrances to their schools and demanded that the French government invest in their educations by increasing staffing, repairing aging buildings and providing more resources to the public education system. Their protests caught the attention of many across the country who were struggling with the high cost of living.

Protest organizers agreed to the plans coordinated with the French government on Saturday, the Interior Ministry said Sunday. But the ministry warned that high-risk groups, largely made up “of radical far-left and ultraleft activists,” had infiltrated demonstrations in medium- and large-sized cities. It blamed those groups for “fomenting attacks” against law enforcement, businesses and other people.

“While the level of violence from these radical elements was the same as last week, their attempted actions — which triggered systematic intervention by law enforcement in line with the clear instructions of the Minister of the Interior — were generally thwarted,” the ministry said.
Richard Engel and Marc Smith reported from Paris and Doha Madani from New York City.
