articles.title: Former RAAF pilot was living 'double life' before wife's death, court hears
articles.author: Tara Cassidy

paras.en: Robert John Crawford is accused of murdering his wife Frances Crawford at their home in 2024 and staging it as an accident.
The Brisbane Supreme Court heard the former RAAF pilot loved money so much "he killed for it".
Mr Crawford has pleaded not guilty to domestic violence murder.
A former RAAF pilot accused of murdering his wife at their Queensland home embarked on a "campaign to make her death appear like a tragic accident", the Brisbane Supreme Court has heard.

On the first day of Robert John Crawford's trial for the alleged murder of his wife Frances Crawford, the court heard he was a "master manipulator", "adulterer and philanderer" who loved money so much he "killed for it".
The former RAAF squadron leader is accused of strangling his wife, and or causing blunt force trauma to her head at their Upper Lockyer home in late July 2024.
The Crown alleged Mr Crawford then manipulated the scene to try and make it appear like she fell while moving their ride-on mower one evening.
On Monday, the court was shown a photo of the mother-of-three's body where it was found beside the mower, which was tipped on its side, next to a retaining wall at their semi-rural property.
According to the prosecution, a "perfect storm" was brewing in the lead up to the alleged murder.
The prosecution said this meant Mr Crawford was due to lose out financially in a divorce settlement, prompted by his infidelity over many years.
"Mr Crawford was interested in other women and not committed to his marriage,"
"He wanted to retain possession and occupancy of their house at Upper Lockyer."

He said Mr Crawford had not wanted to split his lucrative superannuation with his wife in any settlement, and did not like conditions imposed on him during a period the couple were separated and attending counselling, while seeing if they could reconcile the marriage.
The week after Frances Crawford's alleged murder, her husband was due to undergo a "looming" polygraph test and was about to be "booted" out of the couples $2.6 million home, the court heard.
Mr Crawford has pleaded not guilty to one charge of domestic violence murder.
He has been on bail for more than two years as he awaited the trial, which is set down to run for about three weeks.

The jury heard the Crown planned to call nearly 50 witnesses, including the couple's children, Frances Crawford's siblings and friends, first responders, and various forensic, DNA and ecological experts.
A number of Mr Crawford's former RAAF colleagues, and the women he allegedly had relationships and affairs with in the years before his wife's death are also expected to give evidence.
Before her alleged murder in 2024, Frances Crawford worked part time as a psychologist in Toowoomba.
The court heard that she was a devout Christian, and despite wanting "to be loved by her husband" and "live happily ever after like a fairy tale", she instead felt "unsafe" in her marriage.
A number of her loved ones attended court for the first day of the trial, with some to speak as witnesses, while others sat in the public gallery in support of the mother-of-three.

articles.title: Our favourite one-pot pastas for busy weeknights

paras.en: Busy weeknights call for easy meals that don't require much clean up.
We've compiled our favourite one-pot dishes to satisfy the whole family.
Dinner on the table in less than 30 minutes is more than possible with this one-pot pasta — in fact, it's guaranteed.
The pasta soaks up all the flavours as it cooks, and it also creates an irresistibly creamy sauce, thanks to the starchiness of the pasta.
This simple recipe cuts out the need to pre-boil the pasta.
Simply sear the chicken, toss in a pack of store-bought gnocchi, remaining ingredients and bake.
For even less prep, use chicken tenderloins instead of breast fillets.
This easy lemon orzo is packed with lots of spring vegetables, from asparagus to sugar snap peas. And it can be tweaked to your liking.
You can omit vegetables you don't enjoy and add whatever needs using up in your fridge.

Inspired by the Italian dish known as spaghetti all'ubriaco, or "drunken" pasta, this is a one-pot dish in which the pasta is cooked in a red wine bath, which enables the fruity sweetness to permeate each strand of pasta.
The brown butter is the triumphant finish to this beautiful currant-hued dish, with the crispy sage and walnuts bringing irresistible earthy, nutty notes.

articles.title: Patients removed from Canberra health waitlists via letter
articles.author: Penny Travers

paras.en: After waiting years for specialist care through Canberra Health Services (CHS), some patients have found out they have been removed from waitlists via a letter in the mail.
CHS says it is "systematically working through" waitlists, and that the criteria for services like the paediatric allergy clinic had changed.
ACT Opposition Leader Mark Parton says he will move a motion this week calling on the government to "honour the original waiting lists".
When Liz Allen's daughter was seven years old, she suffered an anaphylactic response while helping to peel prawns for a Christmas meal.
She's since had allergic reactions to other unidentified allergens, some of which have involved trips to the emergency department.
In January 2024, Ms Allen said her daughter was referred to Canberra Health Services' paediatric allergy clinic because it was "the best, most comprehensive place" to determine what was going on.

But in mid-October, after almost three years of waiting, she received a letter stating that her daughter had been removed from the waitlist because her condition "no longer meets the requirement for a specialist appointment".
"It is stressful because … it could be life threatening," Ms Allen said.
"Not knowing the source of the allergy is of great concern.
"We have waited on this list patiently in the belief that she would get the medical treatment she needs."
Ms Allen said she received no other communication from Canberra Health Services (CHS) before the letter arrived.
"There was certainly no communication about further information, particularly around her [current] health," she said.
"Each new reaction [she has] occurs about every six months. It is getting more and more of a concern for us as she gets older."
The letter from CHS explained that there were more than 65,000 people on outpatient waiting lists, and that the wait for the allergy centre was more than six years long for some patients.
"To deliver an effective service, the criteria we use to decide which patients can be seen at the clinic has recently been reviewed and updated by our clinicians," the letter stated.

"Our team has reviewed the information your doctor sent us against the new criteria, and your referral no longer meets the criteria for a specialist appointment with CHS, and your referral has been closed."
Ms Allen said it was a "kick in the guts" to have to "start all over again", particularly given their referring doctor had since retired.
"We feel like as family, we are in nowhere land trying to navigate this issue," she said.
A post on social media about her experience attracted dozens of comments from other Canberrans who had received similar letters.
"How is it that the criteria has changed so that even an anaphylactic … response does not make a child eligible for such a service?," she said.
"I do worry about this whole system that appears to be crumbling.
"And that doesn't bode well for families trying to raise healthy children."
CHS 'systematically working through' wait lists

CHS chief operating officer Alison Derritt told 666 ABC Canberra Breakfast that they were "systematically working through" more than 40 outpatient waiting lists as part of a review of specialist and outpatient services.
"There will be more reviews to occur. We are working service by service," she said.
"We need to work through all 40-odd services to understand their waitlists and go through them."
She said the current criteria for the paediatric allergy service was "those under 16 with a severe and complex food allergy, and primarily with the history of anaphylaxis".
"Now we do need to talk to [Liz Allen] ... and certainly happy to understand her particular situation," she said.
"But what we're trying to do is focus on those patients that are at the top categories or top of the new categories and be able to see them in a timely way."
Ms Derritt said that some patients removed from waitlists would need to look at being "seen elsewhere", and one "alternate" would be to go to a private clinic.
She also said some patients needing a "lower category service" may be able to access other local services without needing to travel interstate.

"If someone has got communication or a letter from us and you consider that we've not fully appreciated the situation or there's additional information that you think that we've missed, we're very happy to talk through that with our patients and families," she said.
'Honour original waiting lists': Opposition
ACT Opposition Leader Mark Parton has criticised CHS's process, and accused the government of trying to make waitlists look better.
"We understand that they're going through a process of review, but we don't believe that process of review should mean weeding out everyone on the waiting list and starting from scratch,"
Mr Parton said he would move a motion in the ACT Legislative Assembly this week, calling on the government to "honour the original waiting lists".
"It doesn't matter which way you look at this situation, it's diabolically bad," he said.
"I don't know how the government's going to defend its position because I think it's indefensible.
"And I would hope that the motion that I run tomorrow will give the government the ability to walk back from this and actually genuinely look after the people who need looking after."

articles.title: Carney's geopolitical ambitions tested in defence industry co-operation with Turkey
articles.author: Murray Brewster

paras.en: Carney's geopolitical ambitions tested in defence industry co-operation with Turkey
Developing partnership allows Canada to lessen dependence on U.S. military suppliers

While in Istanbul this past week, Prime Minister Mark Carney struggled for a moment when asked to describe how he felt about limits that had been placed on Ukraine's access to the Starshield military-grade satellite network.
When he found his voice, he spoke about the "immense human suffering" of missile strikes on Kyiv and elsewhere.

"I search for the right adjective to describe whoever took this decision, or a group of people took this decision, against a country — and it's against a country that is literally fighting for the lives of its citizens against naked aggression."
Carney was, however, quick to turn it into an object lesson for Canadians who are skeptical of warming relations with authoritarian-leaning Turkey.

"We as Canadians do not want to be caught in a situation where we are reliant on one provider that may change their view, or may be forced to change their views, by one nation state that puts Canadians at risk — or compromises our sovereignty, our ability to express our values and live our values.”

Early last week, Ukrainian officials said they had lost some of their access to Starshield, the military version of Starlink, the global satellite communications system owned and operated by Elon Musk's company SpaceX.
Ukraine employs Starshield to both track incoming missiles and jet-powered drones, and to guide interceptor and spy drones, while using Starlink for critical internal communications.
Without mentioning the United States or the Trump administration, Carney's reference was clear: We don't want to find ourselves in the same situation as Ukraine.
Canadian officials have made no secret of wanting to reduce reliance on Starlink in favour of a future Telesat system.

Much of Carney’s recent whirlwind trip to Istanbul and the Turkish capital, Ankara, was framed through the lens of the contradiction of values-based Canadians cosying up to a regime that shuts down opposition television stations, arrests journalists and attacks 2SLGBTQ+ advocates.

What was mentioned as part of a strategic partnership signed by Carney — but received far less scrutiny — is the burgeoning defence-industrial co-operation between the two countries, which arguably is an early test of Carney's geopolitical ambitions.

"Canada-Turkey defence co-operation is an early test of whether the middle-power co-ordination the prime minister called for at Davos can produce anything more durable than a sequence of transactions,” wrote Tolga Demiryol, an associate professor of political science at Altınbaş University in Istanbul. He was referring to Carney's speech at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, in January.
A research paper penned by Demiryol was published on the Canadian Global Affairs Institute website in early October.
He said both countries now share a similar outlook when it comes to the defence industry as an instrument of national sovereignty.

"Canada is seeking to reduce the concentration of its defence procurement in the United States, while Turkey's industry was built through repeated efforts to escape foreign control over critical components and export permissions," Demiryol wrote.
"Turkey is courted today for two reasons: it has more to offer than it once did; and Canada has more reason than it once had to look beyond the United States."
Demiryol also said Carney is is not searching "for a replacement partner, but rather to reduce Canadian exposure to any single foreign supplier."
In addition to it being an early test of Carney's middle-power strategy, the defence partnership represents a leap of faith.
Not many years have passed since the events that sent relations between Canada and Turkey into the wilderness.
In 2020, Turkish authorities applied for an exemption related to the importation of target acquisition gear, made by Canadian company Wescam, used in Turkey's Bayraktar drones.
Documents made public stated that Turkish authorities claimed they were using the cameras for reconnaissance activities related to NATO operations in the north of Syria.
But it was later discovered that the cameras were illegally diverted to Azerbaijan and used during the war in Nagorno-Karabakh.
Human rights groups accused Turkey of lying to the Canadian government.
The de facto arms embargo that resulted was lifted in early 2024 when Canada's Department of Foreign Affairs stopped presumptively denying arms export permits to the Middle Eastern country.

While trust has been restored, Carney made clear following talks with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan that the agreement signed on Thursday does not mean unfettered exports and that permits will be reviewed on a case-by-case basis.
"We have standards, we have rules and we will follow them, we will continue to follow them," Carney said.

So what's the attraction of Turkey's defence sector? The short answer is the country's capacity to go from reliance on foreign defence contractors to building its own equipment in a short period of time.

"An important point here, I believe that in Turkey, about 80 per cent of the defence needs of this country are produced here. This is not the case in Canada," Carney said. "So there are a lot of lessons for us on how we can create an industry in our country."
It is also the type of military equipment that Turkey is building that makes it attractive.
A Turkish TB2 drone is seen in Golcuk, Turkey, on Aug. 21. (Burak Kara/Getty Images)

Drones are one example. The TB2, manufactured by Baykar — a private defence and tech company that Carney met with during his stop in Istanbul — proved itself in combat during the opening phase of the war in Ukraine by stopping Russian armoured columns with deadly precision strikes. The country is now manufacturing land and sea drones. It is also developing its own next-generation fighter jet, known as KAAN.

Carney didn't rule out buying Turkish military equipment such as the TB2 but suggested the country's know-how and ability to integrate technologies will be important as Canada expands it own industry.
"We're in a position where we're more in need of Turkish expertise in terms of reinforcing what we need to do to protect Canadians and to serve as a full NATO ally at this stage," Carney said.
Mike Ward, executive director of the Canada Turkey Business Council, said direct investment is another attractive aspect for the prime minister.
Last year, four major Turkish defence companies visited the Toronto Global Forum and pitched investment in Canada's aerospace sector, among others.
"They said, 'Look, we want to do business with Canada. And sure ... Canadian companies can invest in Turkey if you'd like. But we really want to invest in Canada,'" Ward said.
"And those companies have been back. So they're looking to invest. They're looking to invest in Ontario. They're looking to invest to Quebec."
In Europe, Baykar finalized the purchase of an Italian aerospace company, Piaggio, in June 2025. It is also in joint partnership with that country's leading aircraft maker, Leonardo, to build drones.
Demiryol, of Altınbaş University, said he sees shared production and joint rights as a possible way ahead for Canada and Turkey in this new relationship.
But he said transparency will be key to making it work and avoiding the issues that led to the breakdown in relations.

articles.title: Serbia's longtime strongman Vučić concedes election defeat to student-led opposition

paras.en: Serbia's longtime strongman Vučić concedes election defeat to student-led opposition
Streets of Belgrade erupted in celebration after ex-leader's announcement
Serbia's Aleksandar Vučić conceded defeat to a student-led protest movement in a historic election on Sunday that ends his long grip on power and heralds a new political era in the Balkan country.
Vučić, a populist and nationalist, has dominated Serbian politics as prime minister or president since 2014.

But he called a snap election in September after almost two years of student-led demonstrations against perceived corruption and creeping authoritarianism triggered by the deaths of 16 people when a train station canopy collapsed in the city of Novi Sad in 2024.
"It is clear that we have lost these elections, the Student List has won,' Vučić said in a televised speech.
Within moments of his announcement, the streets of the capital, Belgrade, erupted in celebration after Vučić's announcement, with cars honking and students shouting "victory" and "he's done."
The students' win marks a profound political shift in the country of some six million people and is reminiscent of the defeat of Hungary's Viktor Orbán in April.

It may also offer a blueprint for other student movements across Europe, which have taken to the streets in recent weeks to protest — in some cases violently — against poor education standards and a lack of prospects.
Vučić said the students would have between 135 and 140 seats in the 250-seat parliament and that his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) will have 105, based on preliminary results.

"Dear Serbia, tonight the voice of the people is being heard," said Radomir Sajcic, a professor at Belgrade University, speaking on behalf of the students at their headquarters. "Tonight we celebrate victory, tomorrow we build the future."

Lines of unprecedented length had snaked from polling stations in cities and towns across the country earlier in the day, and even Vučić waited for nearly two hours to vote in Belgrade. Pollsters and the election commission put turnout at close to 70 per cent, the highest since the breakup of Yugoslavia in 1992.
"[The turnout] did not surprise me because there was a large and strong mass that has formed throughout the past two years," voter Katarina Petrovic said.
People line up outside a polling station in Belgrade on Sunday. (Armin Durgut/The Associated Press)
Vučić, who resigned from his second term as president to run again for prime minister, was a strong incumbent, and few in the student protest movement dared believe that he would concede so fast.
Supporters credit him with modernizing Serbia's economy and building new highways, railways, schools and hospitals.
"Some businessmen, some people will leave us, but our structure is firm, we are very united, very strong, we are used to being in the opposition," Vučić said.
Much remains unclear about how the student-backed candidates will fare.

Their list of 250 largely unknown personalities includes university professors, actors and farmers, and is led by cardiologist Ilija Srdanovic, although it is still unclear who will be prime minister.

The students' domestic agenda aims to root out graft and improve schooling. Political analysts predict some kind of purge of Vučić allies in the police, security services and ministries. But the students have been quieter on their international ambitions.

As Vučić did for years, they will have to juggle relations with China, a major investor; Russia, Serbia's traditional ally and principal supplier of natural gas; and the European Union, Serbia's largest trading partner.

The student-led street protests, sparked by the station disaster, started small but quickly became the biggest in a generation, calling for Vučić to step down. Rights groups and activists say repression has worsened in the period since.

"For decades the people have been waiting for this time, something to bring hope that we can live freely and by the rules of democracy," actor Jelena Stupljanin, 48, said at a Belgrade polling station.
A voter casts a ballot into a box at a polling station in Belgrade on Sunday. (Marko Djurica/Reuters)

Vučić and his Serbian Progressive Party repeatedly denied accusations of repression, corruption and spying on their opponents. He said the students are funded by foreign agents in Croatia and Montenegro, a charge the students dismiss.

Meanwhile, on the streets of Belgrade, a traditional brass band struck up, and a group including a man in a "students are champions" jumper floated balloons in the shape of the number 3, representing the number of the students' list of candidates.
"We will drink a beer to celebrate, we will get drunk, we are so happy, I have no words to describe how much," said Andjela, a student who was with a group of friends.

articles.title: Lula re-elected in Brazil as Bolsonaro rejects results

paras.en: Lula re-elected in Brazil as Bolsonaro rejects results
Result keeps some distance between Latin America's biggest economy and Washington

Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, a vocal critic of U.S. President Donald Trump, was re-elected on Sunday in a result that keeps some distance between Latin America's biggest economy and Washington.

With 100 per cent of the vote counted, Brazil's electoral court announced that Lula, who turns 81 on Tuesday, had a lead of nearly 4.4 million votes — 51.8 per cent of the total vote — over opponent Flávio Bolsonaro.
The announcement capped an evening of chaos at polling places across Brazil, following a last-minute decision to extend voting by two hours.

Late Sunday, Bolsonaro refused to concede defeat, calling the move to extend voting hours unprecedented — though both he and Lula made the request — and asked for the election results to be annulled, saying they were impossible to accept.
In addressing supporters, Lula expressed his gratitude to the Brazilian people and pledged to respect all Brazilians, regardless of gender or religion. He also attacked Bolsonaro.
Lula supporters celebrate election results in Sao Paulo on Sunday. (Amanda Perobelli/Reuters)
"This was a defeat for denialism and lies. I must confess that every time I attended a debate, I felt embarrassed," he said.
Lula also doubled down on his commitment to Brazil's sovereignty.
"Either the homeland remains free or we die for Brazil," he said. "This country will not accept being anyone's backyard."

Lula's triumph bucks a trend in Latin America where increasing numbers of right-of-centre presidential candidates allied with Trump have been winning, further extending the United States' influence in the region.

His victory leaves Mexico and Brazil, Latin America's two most populous nations, with left-of-centre leaders. It also positions the region's largest economy, with a GDP of $2.6 trillion US per year, to remain independent of the U.S., despite the pressure of increased tariffs imposed by Trump.

A video published by Lula's campaign shows the veteran leader celebrating with his wife, Rosângela Lula da Silva, and allies after his run-off victory was confirmed by Brazil's electoral court. Wearing star-shaped red glasses, he kissed his wife. Hundreds of his supporters began gathering on São Paulo's main artery to celebrate the victory.

In Rio de Janeiro, cars beeped their horns and a woman dressed in red — the colour of Lula supporters — shouted "You lost! Cry harder!" to four men in yellow and green sipping beers, Bolsonaro's signature colours. A huge roar echoed in the street as the result was confirmed.
Lula's supporters celebrate in Rio de Janeiro on Sunday. (Lucas Landau/The Associated Press)

Rodrigo Valentim, a 51-year-old businessman and supporter of Bolsonaro, said that another Lula government would harm the economy. He pointed to financial markets' positive reaction to the result of the first round, when Bolsonaro bested Lula.
"I don't understand how people can vote for Lula," he said. "The country is collapsing."

The electoral court's announcement ended an evening of confusion at polling places after Brazilian Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin ruled three minutes before the scheduled end of voting to keep polls open for two more hours, following requests by both candidates.

Lula's request came after issues with buses that provide transportation to polls in São Paulo and Salvador, two cities that tend to favour the incumbent. Bolsonaro's request was due to heavy rains in Brazil's south, where he is favoured.

In Brasilia, volunteers who oversaw the vote count at a school debated whether they needed to stay after the announcement to extend voting, but most left 15 to 20 minutes after polls closed and they had given count information to electoral authorities.
People line up outside a polling station in Rio de Janeiro on Sunday. (Agustin Marcarian/Reuters)
At a polling station in Rio de Janeiro, the voting machines had already been switched off minutes after polls were set to close and couldn't be turned back on.
The decision delayed tallying the votes by two hours. It was unclear how many polling stations stayed open after the scheduled closing time.
Bolsonaro ally Nikolas Ferreira noted that Zanin, who made the decision, is Lula's former lawyer.
Cost of living, security top of mind for voters

Bolsonaro bested Lula by more than 2.2 million votes in the first round of the election earlier this month. Sunday night's apparent victory by Lula marked the first time since Brazil's military dictatorship ended in 1985 that the second-highest vote-getter in the first-round elections won the presidency.

Lula faced a tough re-election battle because of concerns about the cost of living and security. Bolsonaro made a tough-on-crime approach the cornerstone of his campaign and pledged to bring down food costs, while Lula, trying to lure undecided voters, has invested in costly incentives.
Presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro walks toward a voting booth at a polling station in Rio de Janeiro on Sunday. (Mauro Pimentel/AFP/Getty Images)

Both have been hit by corruption suspicions involving family members and allies, with Bolsonaro implicated in a sprawling scandal rocking Brazil. Lula previously spent more than a year in prison on corruption convictions that were eventually annulled.

This will likely be the last victory of the veteran leader's political career. Lula began his political career in the 1970s as a union leader. He then helped found the Workers' Party, which he represented as a presidential candidate three times until he finally won in 2002. He was re-elected four years later and was succeeded by one of his cabinet ministers, Dilma Rousseff, in 2010. She was re-elected in 2014.

Rousseff was impeached for accounting manoeuvring in 2016 amid a sprawling corruption probe, which also ensnared Lula. He tried to run for president again in 2018 but was jailed in March after being convicted.
Members of the military police stand guard as people gather to watch election results in São Paulo on Sunday. (Jean Carniel/Reuters)

Lula was released from prison after 580 days and saw Brazil's Supreme Court annul his sentence after police found messages that showed the judge who convicted him was biased. He quickly became one of former president Jair Bolsonaro's biggest critics and narrowly beat him in 2022.

Since he lost the first round, Lula reorganized his campaign, appealed to young voters, put millions of Brazilians on the streets to defend democratic values and his legacy, raised fears of another Bolsonaro administration and boosted several government initiatives.
He joins Trump and Nicaraguan President Daniel Ortega — all aged 80 — as the oldest presidents in the Americas.

articles.title: In Bulgaria, record low voter turnout triggers a November 1 presidential run-off in a poll colored by divisions over Ukraine war

paras.en: Record low turnout in Sunday's Bulgarian elections mean voters are expected to head to the polls on November 1 to cast ballots in a presidential run-off.
Polling stations opened at 7 a.m. and closed at 8 p.m. (0500-1800 GMT), with official results expected within 48 hours, but voter turnout was less than 40%, far short of the 50% required.

Voters were choosing between candidates with vastly different views of the war in Ukraine and relations with Moscow and the vote came as drone attacks on ships in the Black Sea off the Bulgarian coast brought home the significance of the conflict in Ukraine for the former Soviet satellite state.

Although the presidency is largely ceremonial, the head of state in Bulgaria can appoint interim governments during political crises, is commander-in-chief of the armed forces and is able to veto legislation.
Who are the main candidates in Bulgaria's presidential election?

Frontrunner in the elections is incumbent President Iliana Yotova, who took over the position this year after current Prime Minister Rumen Radev stepped down to take part in the parliamentary elections that led him to power.
Yotova, 62, who surveys show as having 41-47% of the vote, favors dialogue with Moscow as the way to bring peace to Ukraine and opposes military aid to Kyiv.
A win for Yotova would give a boost for Radev, who also advocates dialogue with Moscow. Victory would make Yotova Bulgaria’s first elected female president.
Her main challenger is Andrey Gyurov, a former caretaker prime minister, who is polling at 28-31%.

Gyurov, 50, who is backed by the pro-Western opposition, is an outspoken critic of Radev's foreign policy and strongly supports the Euro-Atlantic ties of Bulgaria, a European Union and NATO member state. As caretaker prime minister, Gyurov signed a security cooperation agreement with Kyiv.
The leader of the pro-Russian far-right Vazrazhdane party, Kostadin Kostadinov, is in third place on 10-13%.
Altogether 27 pairs of candidates for president and vice president are competing in the first round, with nearly half of them openly pro-Kremlin.

After casting her ballot in Sofia, Yotova called for peace, stability and unity, urging an end to divisions among Bulgarians. Her main challenger, Gyurov, voted in Blagoevgrad, calling for a Bulgaria that looks ahead and offers families greater economic security.
Turnout was estimated at 15.1% by 3 p.m. local time (1300 GMT), according to polling agency Myara, Bulgarian media reported.
To win outright, a candidate must secure more than half the valid votes, with more than half of eligible voters taking part. Otherwise, the top two candidates advance to a runoff on November 1.
What are the main issues in Bulgaria's presidential election?

The war in Ukraine triggered by Russia's unprovoked invasion is one of the central themes in the election, particularly after four merchant ships were allegedly hit by drones off Bulgaria's coast this month in suspected spillover from the conflict. The attacks have prompted Bulgaria to seek assistance from its allies to strengthen maritime security.
Satellite internet antennas from the Starlink network — an important part of Ukraine's defense capabilities — were also set on fire near the capital, Sofia.
While Radev has said that the attacks seemed to be to the advantage of Russia and summoned the Russian ambassador, his government has declined to blame the incidents directly on Moscow.
The strikes have nonetheless raised concerns over Russia’s intentions to escalate the conflict.
Rising energy prices and inflation that have caused economic hardship to many in Bulgaria, the EU's poorest member state, are also a main issue addressed by candidates.
Many voters are also looking to stop government corruption, a persistent concern in the country, and hope for a stable government after multiple elections and coalition breakdowns in recent years.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia looks to US for an AI edge as Yemen's Houthis up pressure

paras.en: Under attack from the militant Houthi group in neighboring Yemen, Saudi Arabia has asked numerous allies for help.
That includes the United States, even though media report that US President Donald Trump refused when Saudi ruler Mohammed bin Salman asked him to take direct military action against the Houthis.

However the US is providing Saudi Arabia with intelligence, which includes a targeting tool that uses artificial intelligence, or AI. A September report by US broadcaster CNN, quoting several unnamed American officials, said that between 100 and 200 US soldiers were in Saudi Arabia as part of new joint force command to facilitate this.
The US personnel were helping the Saudis "use a targeting tool that allows military officers to see in real-time what is happening on the battlefield," CNN reported.
Officials said the system in Saudi Arabia was similar to that known as the Maven Smart System, or MSS for short, which the US military has also used as it sought targets in Iran, Iraq and Syria.

MSS came out of what's known as Project Maven, the US's flagship artificial intelligence program for the military, first launched in 2017. MSS itself is an AI-enabled digital platform that "aggregates, organizes and visualizes vast streams of intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance data," analysts at the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington explained in a June text.

The software system identifies patterns in data coming from, for example, live satellite feeds or drone cameras and then labels potential targets such as possible rocket launchers, tanks or suspicious vehicle convoys.

Previously human military analysts would have had to look at a wide array of different sources to try to find those, the CSIS researchers wrote. It was difficult and, in the case of hours of satellite or drone footage, almost impossible. But MSS now brings hundreds of sources together, analyses them all, then flags possible targets. It also calculates the best method of hitting the target.
Tech commentator Bilawal Sidhu, a former Google product manager, has described the MSS set up as like a "Google Earth for war."
Using the MSS dramatically speeds up what is known as "the kill chain" — that is, the time it takes to detect a target, decide if it's dangerous and then order a strike.

When the US military used MSS while attacking Iran in late February, the AI-powered system facilitated hits on more than 1,000 targets within the first 24 hours of the war. Previously American soldiers were hitting about 100 targets a day.
Up until recently, the long-simmering civil war in Yemen had been comparatively calm following an informal ceasefire negotiated in 2022.

The Houthi rebel group has held large parts of northern and western Yemen since 2015. Yemen's internationally recognized government and other groups held territory across the south and east. That latter is supported by Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.

The Houthi's latest military campaign, which began in September, has seen the group take further control of Yemen's coast. They also ramped up attacks against Saudi Arabia again, hitting the country's main airport and oil facilities. So far, though, military campaigns against the Houthi group by Saudi Arabia, the United States and others have all failed to significantly weaken the group.

This is partially because the Houthis take a "zero-sum approach," Farea al-Muslimi, a research fellow focused on Yemen at UK think tank Chatham House, told DW recently. The group's founding father argued that contemporary Muslim societies were too "soft," and that poverty and hardship are a divine test, al-Muslimi said.
"They don't care if the Israelis bomb the airport or the US bombs a hospital," the expert said. "It actually serves them very well because their ideology is all about martyrdom and sacrifice."
There are certain technical issues users have noted with the MSS in the past that could also prove problematic in Yemen.

The Houthis tend to be highly mobile, using truck-mounted ballistic missiles and small drone swarms as they operate from hills and canyons in rugged countryside. It's possible that fighters might be long gone before they can be attacked even with the help of AI-assisted targeting.

Though MSS is known to work best in relatively unpopulated areas, factors such as changes in desert terrain, dust storms, high wind, snowfall and dense foliage — and even deliberately planted decoys — can reduce its success rate.
There is also a worrying ethical aspect to shortening the kill chain. A human is always supposed to verify the target that the AI-assisted tool has identified and decide how to react.

But it doesn't always work that way. For example, among the sites MSS targeted in Iran on the first day of the war was a school. An American missile killed almost 200 people at a primary school in southern Iran, most of them children aged between seven and 12.

In its military campaign in Gaza, Israel — arguably the Middle Eastern country with the most advanced military-use AI — has also used AI-assisted targeting. An Israeli system known as the Gospel, or Habsora, is the closest to MSS in the way it works.

But, as has been documented elsewhere, including by Israeli and British journalists and in the recent documentary Naza, the use of such AI targeting tools have also been highly problematic because of the numbers of civilian casualties that can result.

"On the one hand [in Gaza], AI has enhanced commanders' situational awareness, lessened the human costs of tunnel mapping, improved the speed of military strikes, and boosted the survivability of troops," analysts Frederic Wehrey and Andrew Bonney wrote for War on the Rocks, a specialist media outlet. "Yet the benefits afforded by such functions have been overshadowed by mounting civilian deaths reportedly resulting from this technology's safeguards being loosened or eliminated."

All of which is why Antony Loewenstein, an independent journalist based in Australia who has researched the impact of Israel's AI-assisted technology, doesn't believe similar technology will lead to the defeat of the Houthi group.

"I don't think there's much evidence at all that using an AI tool is going to make much difference on the ground, except for causing huge amounts of civilian casualties," Loewenstein, who authored the book, "The Palestine Laboratory: How Israel Exports The Technology of Occupation Around the World," told DW. "And I think what the US and the Saudis will find is that the Houthis have an incredibly high tolerance level for destruction."

articles.title: Uganda says it has no active Ebola cases, but infections in Kenya and Nigeria are prompting fresh scrutiny

paras.en: The first confirmed Ebola patients in Kenya and Nigeria may have crossed paths at Uganda's Entebbe International Airport, according to African health officials, as new information from Switzerland contradicts Uganda's account of the Nigerian patient's travel history.
Uganda, a country reporting no active Ebola infections, has become a focus of investigations into cases thousands of kilometers apart.

Uganda insists that it has no confirmed active cases of the deadly virus. Yet health authorities in Kenya and Nigeria are investigating Ebola infections involving people whose travel histories or contacts are connected to the East African nation.

Both patients passed through Entebbe International Airport on October 3, according to Wessam Mankoula, head of emergency preparedness and response at the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC).
Health officials say the two may have crossed paths, although it has not been established whether they encountered each other or whether any transmission occurred at the airport.

The differing accounts have raised questions about whether Uganda was simply a transit point for infected travelers. Or could infections be going undetected along some of Africa's busiest cross-border routes?
The latest developments come after Switzerland disputed claims that the Nigerian patient had visited the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), where an Ebola outbreak is underway.
Did the two Ebola patients cross paths in Uganda?
Nigerian Health Minister Muhammad Ali Pate confirmed an Ebola case in the capital, Abuja, involving a woman who had recently traveled to East Africa, including Uganda.
"Today we are confirming that there has been one imported case of Ebola virus disease in the Federal Capital Territory," Pate said.
The woman developed symptoms on October 7 and visited a private health facility on October 11. Further laboratory testing confirmed Ebola, and she was subsequently isolated for treatment.
Pate said the patient was stable and health officials had identified 44 contacts, including health care workers, caregivers, patients and people who may have encountered her during her travels.
But the woman's journey has become central to the investigation.

Speaking on Thursday, Mankoula said the first confirmed patients in Kenya and Nigeria were both known to have traveled through Entebbe International Airport on October 3. Investigators are examining whether the two patients were at the airport at the same time and whether their movements overlapped.
Switzerland contradicts Uganda's account
Uganda's Health Ministry says preliminary findings indicate that the Nigerian patient traveled to eastern DRCfor business before passing through Uganda without symptoms and returning to Nigeria.
"Travel through Uganda does not establish that infection occurred here. The location of exposure remains under investigation," the ministry said in an October 20 statement.
But, on Friday, Switzerland's Federal Department of Foreign Affairs directly disputed the account.
"She and her husband did not travel to the Democratic Republic of the Congo," the department said in a statement to Reuters news agency.
The woman, identified by Swiss authorities as a Swiss national of Ugandan origin, is married to a Swiss diplomat based in Abuja.

On Thursday, the Swiss government told Reuters that she was believed to have contracted Ebola while traveling with her husband in Uganda, although that assessment has not been independently confirmed.
The World Health Organization (WHO) and the Africa CDC also said Thursday that they had not received confirmed information establishing that the woman had traveled to the DRC.

The conflicting accounts raise fresh questions about where the woman was exposed to the virus and how accurately her movements were initially reconstructed. They do not, however, establish that she contracted Ebola in Uganda.
Uganda maintains that it has no confirmed active Ebola cases and says it is awaiting more detailed information from Nigeria about the woman's movements.
Kenya's missing contact complicates investigation

In Kenya, Uganda has emerged in a separate investigation involving the country's first confirmed Ebola patient, who died in the Kenyan capital, Nairobi, on October 5. The patient had traveled from the Democratic Republic of Congo through Uganda before reaching Kenya.

Health officials have now established that the patient passed through Entebbe International Airport on October 3, the same day as the woman subsequently diagnosed in Nigeria. Kenyan authorities have since reported additional infections linked to the initial case.
But one aspect of the investigation remains unresolved.
According to Kenya's Daily Nation, health officials are searching for a Ugandan national identified as a contact of the deceased patient.
"We know him (the Ugandan) by name and passport number and from his phone but we are not able to reach him," Kenya's director-general for health, Patrick Amoth, told the newspaper.
The Daily Nation reported that the man was using a South Sudanese telephone number, complicating efforts to establish his whereabouts.
Being an untraced contact does not mean that he is infected. However, locating potentially exposed individuals is essential to preventing further transmission.
Uganda shares a lengthy border with the Democratic Republic of Congo, where Ebola outbreaks have repeatedly challenged health authorities.
Cross-border trade, population movements and international travel make it difficult to establish where someone was exposed to the virus.
Ebola symptoms typically develop two to 21 days after infection. According to the WHO, people infected with Ebola are not considered infectious until symptoms appear.
Even well-functioning border surveillance systems cannot identify every infected traveler.

The discovery that both patients traveled through the same international airport on the same day illustrates the complexity of tracing potential exposures across multiple countries. It also highlights the importance of reconstructing travel histories and identifying close contacts.
Uganda says it is strengthening screening and public health controls at points of entry. Nigeria has intensified contact tracing and infection prevention measures.
The challenge is ensuring that authorities across different countries can exchange accurate information quickly enough to identify potential exposures.

In Abuja, the confirmed infection has revived memories of previous Ebola outbreaks. Resident Peace Kolawole expressed concern about the consequences of another outbreak. "So here is my hand sanitizer, so I'm actually very concerned about it," she told DW.

Others fear that Nigeria's health care system may struggle to respond while many citizens face economic hardship. "Because now people are not even worried about sickness anymore, people are worried about surviving," Abuja resident Jonathan Steven told DW.
Nigeria's health authorities say the patient is receiving medical care and contact tracing is continuing.
Uganda's position between the DRC and other regional destinations offers one explanation for its appearance in both investigations.

But the latest findings have added two significant questions: Did the patients from Kenya and Nigeria come into contact at Entebbe International Airport on October 3? And where did the Nigerian woman contract the virus if, as Switzerland insists, she never traveled to DR Congo?

The conflicting accounts from Uganda and Switzerland have made establishing the Nigerian patient's travel history an urgent part of the investigation. The WHO and Africa CDC have yet to confirm the disputed DR Congo travel history.
Uganda's declaration of zero confirmed active cases does not establish that all infections have been ruled out. Equally, the travel histories do not prove an undetected outbreak.

For Kenya and Nigeria, the immediate priority is containing confirmed infections. For Uganda, the challenge is demonstrating that its surveillance systems are effective and reassuring both its citizens and neighboring countries.
The Africa CDC will convene an "extraordinary virtual meeting" of national health officials on October 28 as the continent's latest Ebola outbreak continues to spread.

articles.title: US military says it helped Gulf states export 1.5 billion barrels of oil

paras.en: US military forces have helped Gulf countries export more than 1.5 billion barrels of oil since June, despite Iran’s efforts to control the critical waterway, according to US Central Command (COMMAND).
The US military command said on Sunday that more than 3,000 commercial vessels had transited the Strait of Hormuz with its support over the past six months.

It added that more than 95 percent of ships navigating the channel had sailed through safely in recent months despite Iranian threats, “clearly demonstrating that the United States and regional partners control the international waterway”.

CENTCOM announced the figures as Commander Admiral Brad Cooper made a visit to the region, during which he observed the “current operational environment” in the strait while flying in a US Army helicopter.
“We continue to stand shoulder to shoulder with our Gulf partners and the shipping industry,” Cooper said in a statement.
“This visit underscores our strong commitment to continued freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz.”
Cooper said the primary transit routes for vessels in the strait were free of Iranian mines due to the “incredible efforts” of personnel who conduct mine clearance operations.
“We remain intensely focused on keeping commercial traffic flowing as we work with our teammates in the US interagency, Gulf Cooperation Council, and shipping industry,” he said.

Crude oil flows have largely returned to levels seen before the US and Israel launched their war on Iran in late February, despite the ongoing threat of attacks on commercial vessels by Iranian forces.
At least 16.5 million barrels of oil per day left the region in September, equal to the pre-war average, excluding Iran, according to market intelligence firm Kpler.
Analysts have attributed the rebound to a combination of offshore ship-to-ship transfers, US military escorts, and increased use of oil pipelines.
However, oil prices remain far higher than before the start of the war.
Brent crude futures stood at about $114.50 a barrel on Sunday, after easing about 2 percent from last week’s nearly six-month high.
Brent settled at $72.48 per barrel on February 27, the day before the US and Israel began strikes on Iran.

articles.title: Attackers kill nurse, injure health worker responding to DRC Ebola case

paras.en: A nurse has been killed and another health worker severely injured after they were attacked while responding to an Ebola alert in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), according to the World Health Organization.
It was the latest in a series of attacks on health workers and responders that authorities say is hampering efforts to slow the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in the world.
The attack took place on Saturday in the town of Bafwasende in the DRC’s eastern Tshopo province, WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said in a post on X on Sunday.
“Everyone working to protect communities from this deadly disease must be able to work in dignity and safety. Healthcare must always be protected,” he said.
The WHO’s regional director for Africa, Dr Mohamed Yakub Janabi, also condemned the attack on X.
“Health is NOT a target,” he said. “Those responding to the Ebola outbreak must be protected. Misinformation and fear must never fuel violence.”
Local authorities have not yet commented on the attack or the suspects.

Data from the DRC’s Ministry of Health indicate that more than 9,800 cases, including more than 4,700 deaths, have been recorded since the start of the outbreak in May, making it the deadliest Ebola outbreak in the country’s history.
The government’s handling of the outbreak, combined with chronic corruption, has sown widespread distrust, with some even dismissing Ebola as a hoax.

Responders say scepticism about the disease among communities has complicated their efforts, including in remote areas and emerging hotspots already facing shortages of medical supplies and healthcare workers.

Last month, a DRC politician was beaten to death in North Kivu after publicly defending the government’s response to Ebola. He had called on the public to obey response measures, particularly social distancing and hand-washing, on a radio show.
In May, at the start of the outbreak, angry residents set alight two tents at health centres in two separate attacks in just one week.
Responders say some residents have held captive or threatened team members in designated health zones.
The current outbreak has now been reported in four countries across eastern, central and western Africa, giving it the widest geographic spread of any Ebola outbreak on the continent to date.
On Sunday, Uganda’s Minister of Health Chris Baryomunsi announced that all citizens returning to the country with a history of travel to the DRC will be quarantined for 21 days.

Uganda says it is Ebola-free after declaring an end to its latest outbreak in July. But health experts remain on alert after two people who had recently passed through the country later tested positive in Kenya and Nigeria.
Ebola spreads through direct contact with the bodily fluids of infected people.
The strain responsible for the current outbreak, known as Bundibugyo, has no approved vaccine or specific treatment.

Symptoms can take up to 21 days to appear, according to the WHO. In an October 23 update, it urged stronger monitoring and cooperation across borders, while advising against restrictions on travel or trade with affected countries.

articles.title: US appeals court sceptical of Trump’s lawsuit over California voter rolls

paras.en: A United States appeals court has expressed doubt over the Department of Justice’s lawsuit against California, which seeks to force the state to throw out mail-in ballots it has deemed likely to go to non-citizens.
Circuit Judge Mark Bennett said on Sunday that the three-judge panel would issue a decision as soon as possible, following a rare weekend oral argument.
But Bennett, an appointee of Republican President Donald Trump, voiced concern that the lawsuit would not hold up to scrutiny.
He pointed to the Elections Clause in the US Constitution, which allows states — not the federal government — to administer elections.

“It seems to me that you want us to issue an injunction that is entirely inconsistent with the law that the California legislature has adopted pursuant to the Elections Clause,” Bennett told Justice Department lawyer Matthew Donnelly. “How can we do that?”
The case is part of a larger effort under the right-wing Trump administration to crack down on alleged non-citizen voting ahead of the crucial November 3 midterm elections.
On October 15, less than three weeks before the midterm races, the Justice Department issued a complaint targeting California, a left-wing stronghold.
It asked the federal court system to set aside thousands of mail-in ballots that the government says were sent to “likely non-citizens”.
The lawsuit indicates the Trump administration sent California officials a list of 20,000 names it believes are not eligible to vote, based on citizenship.
Trump has often pushed the discredited claim that the Democratic Party is benefiting from widespread voting by non-citizens.
California has long been one of the targets for his election misinformation.
Earlier this year, Trump denounced the state’s primaries after right-wing candidates like Los Angeles mayoral hopeful Spencer Pratt felt short of his expectations.
“There’s BIG cheating by the Dumocrats in California,” he wrote on social media at the time.
He then announced that the state would be under investigation from the US attorney’s office.
Trump’s efforts have caused alarm, with critics accusing him of seeking to dampen voter turnout through intimidation and confusion.
The midterms will decide which party controls the US Congress, as well as key state and local positions.
Polls, however, predict steep odds for Republican candidates, given Trump’s souring approval ratings and dissatisfaction with issues like the cost of living and the US-Israeli war against Iran.

Voting rights advocates have warned that the Trump administration has not publicly revealed how it has compiled its list of non-citizen voters, and whistleblower reports have cast doubt on the accuracy of such lists.
In response to the October 15 lawsuit, California has countered that it has strong safeguards to prevent non-citizens from voting.
It also said that the Justice Department’s claims are based on dubious data.

“This is a sad, desperate attempt by Trump to use his politicized Justice Department to try to suppress California voters just three weeks before Election Day,” California Governor Gavin Newsom said in a statement earlier this month.
“We will continue to carry out free and fair elections in the Golden State — and call out this authoritarian as he tries every play in the dictator’s playbook.”

articles.title: This center-right former general could unseat Netanyahu as Prime Minister in Israel
articles.author: Daniel Estrin

paras.en: This center-right former general could unseat Netanyahu as Prime Minister in Israel
A former Israeli general is the main center-right challenger hoping to unseat Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in Israeli elections this week.

Benjamin Netanyahu is Israel's longest-serving prime minister - more than 19 years if you add up all the terms he's served. This week, he's battling to stay in power. On Tuesday, Israelis go to the polls after years of wars across the region. NPR's Daniel Estrin is in Israel and has this story on the former general trying to unseat Netanyahu and his far-right government.
UNIDENTIFIED PERSON: No. 1, Gadi Eisenkot, yeah.
DANIEL ESTRIN, BYLINE: Gadi Eisenkot is Netanyahu's leading opponent. At a stump speech a few weeks ago, I watch him take the stage. He's a short man with cropped white hair, wearing all black.
GADI EISENKOT: (Non-English language spoken).

ESTRIN: The event is in Kiryat Gat, a city near the Gaza border. Historically, it's a conservative Netanyahu stronghold. This crowd knows Eisenkot as the former military chief of staff appointed by Netanyahu a decade ago. He came back into the public spotlight days after Hamas attacked Israel on October 7, 2023. He joined Netanyahu's war Cabinet. Very soon, the nation saw Eisenkot crying over his son's casket.
EISENKOT: (Non-English language spoken).

ESTRIN: His son was a soldier killed in Gaza. The very next day, his nephew was killed fighting in Gaza. Eisenkot tells this crowd that after the first three months of war, he thought things were going in the wrong direction.
EISENKOT: (Non-English language spoken).

ESTRIN: "I saw a deep dysfunction in the decision-making process," he says. "I saw that political and personal considerations were put above everything else." He means Netanyahu. He's pledging to voters the first thing he'll do as prime minister is to do the thing Netanyahu has refused to do, to launch an official national investigation into the security failure of October 7.
EISENKOT: (Non-English language spoken).
ESTRIN: In the crowd, I met Yair Amar. He told me he always used to vote for "Bibi" - Benjamin Netanyahu.
YAIR AMAR: (Non-English language spoken).
ESTRIN: But he says Netanyahu is responsible for all the Israelis killed on October 7. And Eisenkot?
ESTRIN: He says, "he's straight" - like a straight shooter, down to earth. He's everything Netanyahu isn't, says Amos Harel, an Israeli defense analyst for the newspaper Haaretz.

AMOS HAREL: Many Israelis wish for a saner future, for somebody who perhaps is not as charismatic and doesn't look the part of an American senator but is one of us and is seen as somebody who sacrificed a lot.

ESTRIN: The race is very, very tight. Most polls show Eisenkot's camp ahead of Netanyahu's camp. But those same polls show that neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot has a clear path to victory. The election could tip based on a small amount of votes, or it could end in a stalemate and force a repeat election next spring. If that were to happen, Netanyahu would stay in power without a new mandate from the public but with full authority to make fateful decisions like going to war. If Eisenkot wins, he has promised to crack down on settler expansion and violence against Palestinians in the West Bank. He talks about reaching diplomatic agreements in all the wars Netanyahu has kept open. But there's one thing he's made clear. He would not withdraw troops from Lebanon and Gaza anytime soon.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: EISENKOT: (Non-English language spoken).

ESTRIN: "Truth be told," Eisenkot told the crowd, "it will take a lot of time." He said the Israeli military presence in both places is necessary until Hamas and Hezbollah's military forces are dismantled. And on the biggest question of all, how to solve Israel's conflict with the Palestinians...
EISENKOT: (Non-English language spoken).

ESTRIN: ...Eisenkot boasted to the crowd that he never said the solution was two states for two peoples, meaning creating a Palestinian state alongside Israel. That is the vision that the U.S. and the majority of the world has advocated for decades. Eisenkot thinks Israel should preserve possibilities for a solution in the future. After October 7, Israelis do not want to discuss a Palestinian state. Analyst Amos Harel.
HAREL: It's not something that the Israeli public can swallow at this time. More and more people suspect that the Arabs, the Palestinians are out to kill us and that the world is out to get us.

ESTRIN: That mistrust of Arabs has a direct impact on Eisenkot's chances in the race. Polls suggest the opposition parties would easily win if they'd be willing to share power with Arab political parties representing Israel's Arab citizens. But opposition parties say they won't partner with Arab parties, which is a victory for Netanyahu. He's running a campaign claiming the Arab political parties pose a threat, says Harel.

HAREL: The fact that, in spite of his political weakness, Netanyahu managed to reach a sort of a consensus among the Israeli public that the Arab parties, led by Arab Israeli citizens, are illegitimate as partners is quite amazing.

ESTRIN: This is not a race of conservatives versus liberals, right versus left. Eisenkot is leading a group of politicians who are largely right wing - not the far right of Netanyahu's camp, but right wing, focused on boosting Israel's military for whatever dangers are to come and recruiting religious ultra-Orthodox Jews to the military, trying to tell Israelis, it's OK not to vote for Netanyahu. I'll make sure Israel stays strong.
ANAT BEN-ARI: I'm trusting him on the military level, but is it enough?
ESTRIN: High school theater teacher Anat Ben-Ari came to hear Eisenkot speak, and she's almost nervous voicing an unpopular opinion out loud. She thinks he shouldn't shy away from peace agreements.

BEN-ARI: The only way to end war, all the history says that, is by agreements - people talking to people, even enemies, mostly enemies. And I think we should also pay the price for peace in order for less people to die here and not always live on our swords.

ESTRIN: With days to go before elections, war is fresh on Israelis' minds. Netanyahu is campaigning for votes with a new promise. If he wins, he'll partner with the U.S. to launch a new attack on Iran. Daniel Estrin, NPR News, Kiryat Gat in southern Israel.

articles.title: U.S. influence in Latin America at stake in runoff election in Brazil
articles.author: Carrie Kahn

paras.en: U.S. influence in Latin America at stake in runoff election in Brazil

A polarizing presidential election runoff in Latin America's largest economy and biggest democracy pits leftist Lula da Silva's legacy against Trump ally Flavio Bolsonaro, son of the former Brazilian president.

Voting in Brazil's tight presidential runoff election has been extended today. Both candidates asked for that extension. The race to lead Latin America's largest democracy is a nail-biter. Many polls say it's too close to call. Incumbent leftist President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva is facing his toughest election of his long political career. His challenger, Flávio Bolsonaro, is the son of the former far-right president, and he has managed to galvanize Brazilians who've been increasingly voting conservative in recent years. We now go to the capital city Brasília where we are joined by NPR's Carrie Kahn. Hi, Carrie.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: PFEIFFER: Carrie, what is the voting scene like out there today?

KAHN: Well, it had been a very calm day, but busy here in Brasília. Polls were set to close at 5 p.m. local time, but now the Supreme Court has ruled that voting be extended. A justice was acting on separate petitions, as you said, from both candidates' parties. But there's been a lot of confusion because that ruling to extend the hours came just after the polls closed. So some stations reopened, others had turned off voting machines. We'll just have to see how this shakes out in the coming hours.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: PFEIFFER: And tell us about President Lula's challenger, Flávio Bolsonaro.

KAHN: He is a current senator. His father is Jair Bolsonaro, who lost his own reelection bid four years ago to Lula and then was convicted for attempting a coup to overturn that election. Flávio Bolsonaro has done very well in this race. He's 45. He is much younger than Lula, and he's projected himself as a change for Brazil. He's not as bombastic as his father. He's not as charismatic, either, but he did pull out his first-place finish in the first round of voting ahead of Lula.
PFEIFFER: And, Carrie, I assume you've been talking with voters. What are you hearing from them?

KAHN: Yes. I spent a lot of time today at this large private university in a suburb here outside the capital. It had dozens of polling stations. The crowds were big there and constant and much more enthusiastic than during the first round. You know, in that first round, we saw more than 33 million people sit out the vote. Here's a 50-year-old cattle rancher that I spoke to. His name is Flavio - Flavio too - but it's Flavio Coelho. He said he just wants the left out, and Brazil needs a change after so many years of Lula.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: KAHN: He says, "the left hands out high salaries to people who do nothing, who just sit at a desk all day." And he wants to see cuts to Brazil's public sector and programs. He also wants to see closer ties with the U.S. And he wants Bolsonaro to pardon his father and also revamp Brazil's Supreme Court, which he says has become too powerful. And there were plenty of Lula supporters there, too, Sacha.
PFEIFFER: And those Lula supporters, what are they saying?

KAHN: Many were worried about those cuts to social services for the poor and cuts to Brazil's free healthcare, like this Lula voter, Kleber Mendonca. He works for the federal government. He says no one on the left in Brazil could beat Bolsonaro. Lula had to run.
KAHN: He says, "look, Lula is a great leader, a great statesman, and he's been very active for an 80-year-old."

A Lula has been the dominant figure in Brazil's left for more than 25 years. Many voters, though, did say they were ready for better options on both sides. I heard that a lot, that voters have soured on politics here in Brazil, where the only chance for many - the only choice they've had for many years has been either a Bolsonaro or Lula.

PFEIFFER: And right, Carrie, you said many people sat out the last election, but it sounds like today there are voters out in force. It feels like despite political fatigue, they still care. They're still coming to vote.

KAHN: It does feel like the campaign's picked up speed in the final days, holding huge rallies. But many voters say they feel like they're voting for the lesser of two evils. Both candidates face allegations of corruptions during their political careers. Lula was convicted of corruption and spent time in jail. His charges were overturned, and he's always denied wrongdoing. But that stained his legacy.

And Bolsonaro and his family have allegations too. Recently, they've been having to fight back these charges over millions of dollars raised for a biopic about Jair Bolsonaro, and the money came from this disgraced banker. Flávio Bolsonaro denies any wrongdoing. But, you know, all these accusations contribute to voter fatigue and apathy in this really crucial race here in Brazil right now.
PFEIFFER: Carrie, although this is an overseas election, how has the relationship between Brazil and the U.S. and President Trump played into this race?

KAHN: The No. 1 issues are domestic, though, like the high cost of living and crime. But Trump does come up, especially as he's become more assertive in Latin America. For Lula voters, they say they - that worries them, and they don't want the U.S. coming and taking Brazil's resources like its rare earth minerals. Bolsonaro voters, however, applaud the closer ties especially, many say, if that helps combat crime.
PFEIFFER: That is NPR international correspondent Carrie Kahn, speaking to us from Brasília. Thanks, Carrie.
